On posets and polytopes attached to arbors

F. Chapoton
August 24, 2026
Abstract

Starting from the data of an arbor, which is a rooted tree with vertices decorated by disjoint sets, we introduce a lattice polytope and a partial order on its lattice points. We give recursive formulas for various classical invariants of these polytopes and posets, using the tree structure. For linear arbors, we propose a conjecture exchanging the Ehrhart polynomial of the polytope with the Zeta polynomial of the poset for the reverse arbor. The general motivation comes from a transmutation operator acting on MM-triangles, which should link the posets considered here with some kind of generalized noncrossing partitions and generalized associahedra. We give some evidence for this relationship in several cases, including notably some polytopes, namely halohedra and Hochschild polytopes.

À la mémoire des petits bilbis.

Introduction

The combinatorial data that will be our starting point is a rooted tree whose vertices are decorated with a partition of a finite set. Such objects will be called arbors. This article introduces two constructions attached to any arbor tt. The first construction is a lattice polytope QtQ_{t} inside some ℕn\mathbb{N}^{n} and the second one is the partial order PtP_{t} defined by coordinate-wise comparison on the set of lattice points in this polytope.

Before explaining at length the motivation for these constructions coming from Coxeter groups, cluster theory and representation theory, let us describe our results.

First, it is shown that the polytopes QtQ_{t}, initially defined by inequalities, are lattice polytopes, which means that they have integral vertices. Moreover, they are simple polytopes and have no interior lattice point. Their vertices are described in a recursive way, using a projection map π\pi to a product of smaller polytopes in the same family. The polytopes are also identified as Minkowski sums of simplices. Basic properties of the posets PtP_{t} are also stated: they are graded with a unique minimum and the interval between this minimum and any element is a product of total orders. This property allows to view their Hasse diagrams as skeletons of cubical complexes.

Our next set of results consists of recursive formulas to compute several invariants of the polytopes QtQ_{t} and posets PtP_{t}. This uses the projection map π\pi and often requires a finer invariant that includes information about the height, which is the sum of coordinates. A recursive formula is obtained for the Ehrhart polynomial of the polytope QtQ_{t}, which counts lattice points in the dilates, cf. [Bar08]. One considers then the function that measures the volume in the hyperplane sections according to height, and gets recursive formulas for this function and for its Laplace transform. Similarly, recursive formulas are given for the Zeta polynomial, the MM-triangle and the ff-vector of the poset PtP_{t}. The Zeta polynomial is a classical invariant that counts chains in the poset, see [Sta74, §3]. The MM-triangle is a polynomial in two variables, defined in [Cha04] for any graded poset, as a weighted sum of all Möbius numbers, similar to the more classical characteristic polynomial introduced in [Rot64]. The ff-vector is defined by counting faces of the underlying cubical complex.

In Section 3, two conjectures are proposed in the case of linear arbors. The first one claims that reversing the arbor upside-down should exchange the Ehrhart polynomial of the polytope QtQ_{t} and the Zeta polynomial of the poset PtP_{t}. Here both constructions interact in a rather surprising way. The second conjecture claims that the hh-vector is unchanged by reversing a linear arbor. Here the hh-vector of an arbor tt is the generating polynomial of elements of PtP_{t} according to the number of non-zero coordinates.

In Section 4, we introduce transmutation as a birational involution acting on the MM-triangle. Transmutation is central in the original motivation of the article and appears in the results in the next sections. Here the reader may want to read the motivation section below first.

In the five next sections, we gather evidence concerning transmutation for several specific families of arbors. Let us say that two posets are transmuted partners if they share the same Zeta polynomial and their MM-triangles are related by transmutation.

In Section 5, we propose conjectures about unary-binary arbors. In this case, one can define from the arbor tt a gentle quiver-with-relations whose lattice of support τ\tau-tilting objects is finite. Applying the core-label-order construction should lead to transmuted partners of the posets PtP_{t}. This is also stated in the more combinatorial language of Stokes posets for quadrangulations [Bar01, Cha16].

In Section 6, we consider the case of arbors of type 𝔸\mathbb{A}, meaning linear arbors with no multiple vertex. We introduce a more general family of posets, including the posets PtP_{t} for arbors of type 𝔸\mathbb{A}. We compute the Zeta polynomials and the MM-triangles of these more general posets. This implies that noncrossing partitions of Coxeter type 𝔸\mathbb{A} are transmuted partners of the posets PtP_{t} for arbors of type 𝔸\mathbb{A}.

In Section 7, we consider the case of arbors of type 𝔹\mathbb{B}, meaning arbors with only one vertex. We introduce a more general family of posets, including the poset PtP_{t} for arbors of type 𝔹\mathbb{B}. We compute the Zeta polynomials and the MM-triangles of these more general posets. This implies that noncrossing partitions of Coxeter type 𝔹\mathbb{B} are transmuted partners of the posets PtP_{t} for arbors of type 𝔹\mathbb{B}.

In Section 8, we turn to arbors with one simple vertex and one multiple vertex. The aim is to relate them to the family of simple polytopes named halohedra [DHV11, DFHV12]. We prove that the hh-vector of the polytope coincides with the hh-vector of the arbor.

In Section 9, we turn to arbors that are corollas, namely with no multiple vertex and such that all non-root vertices are attached to the root vertex. The aim is to relate these arbors to the family of Hochschild polytopes [San09, RS18] and the associated Hochschild lattices [Com21]. We conjecture that the core-label-orders of Hochschild lattices are transmuted partners of the posets PtP_{t}. We prove that the hh-vector of the Hochschild polytope coincides with the hh-vector of the arbor.

0.1 Motivation

Let us now try to explain, with the help of the following figure, where this work comes from.

Let us start with the leftmost box. The theory of Cambrian lattices [Rea06] defines, for any finite Coxeter group WW and Coxeter element c∈Wc\in W, a finite lattice. For crystallographic simply-laced Coxeter groups, these lattices can also be described inside the theory of cluster algebras, using green mutations, see [KD20] for a survey. There is an alternative representation-theoretic viewpoint using inclusion of torsion classes for finite-dimensional algebras, considered also using support τ\tau-tilting objects [AIR14]. It is known that finite lattices of torsion-classes are congruence-uniform [GM19, DIR+23]. It is also known that Cambrian lattices are congruence-uniform, as quotients of the weak order on the Coxeter group [Rea06].

Let us move to the top box, closely tied to the previous one. It is known that the Hasse diagrams of Cambrian lattices are skeletons of some simple polytopes, sometimes called generalized associahedra [CFZ02]. In this setting, one can define the FF-triangle, a polynomial in two variables that refines the ff-vector of the polytope [Cha04] and depends on the choice of a distinguished vertex. Its definition, as recalled in Appendix A, is applied to the polar polytope seen as a spherical simplicial complex with a distinguished facet.

Consider now the bottom box. Starting from a congruence-uniform lattice in the leftmost box, one can define another lattice, using the canonical join representation. This construction was introduced by Reading in [Rea16, §9.7] under the name of shard-intersection-order. This is also known as the core-label-order, in the terminology of [Müh19]. For Cambrian lattices, the core-label-order only depends on WW and recovers the WW-noncrossing-partitions lattice of Brady-Watt [BW02] and Bessis [Bes15]. As these lattices are graded, one can define their MM-triangles as recalled in Appendix A.

In the Cambrian context, the FF-triangle of the generalized associahedra is related to the MM-triangle of the lattice of WW-noncrossing-partitions by the explicit birational transformations (57) and (56) recalled in Appendix A. This equality was conjectured in [Cha04] and proved in [Ath07]. These birational transformations are expected to be more widely applicable in similar contexts, see for example [GM20]. Note that this birational relationship implies that hh-vectors of generalized associahedra also enumerate non-crossing partitions according to their rank.

All this forms a well-traveled landscape, involving congruence-uniform lattices and directed skeletons of polytopes. Our main claim is that there should exist another aspect of this story, related to the previous landscape by transmutation.

The core idea is that some posets from the bottom box (noncrossing partitions and similar posets) should be transmuted partners of some posets from the middle box (associated with arbors). By this expression, we mean that two posets share the same Zeta polynomial and that their MM-triangles are related by an explicit birational involution that we choose to call transmutation.

The starting point for the project was in fact in the other direction: starting from the classical lattices of noncrossing partitions, we have found their transmuted partners. This has led us to the present framework of arbors.

We will prove in Section 6 that for linear arbors in which every vertex has only one element, the transmuted MM-triangle is indeed the MM-triangle of the noncrossing-partitions lattice of type 𝔸\mathbb{A}. Moreover, we prove that they share the same Zeta polynomial, so they are indeed transmuted partners as claimed.

In a similar vein, it is shown in Section 7 that the noncrossing partitions lattices of type 𝔹\mathbb{B} are transmuted partners of the posets PtP_{t} for arbors with one vertex.

♣\clubsuit ♣\clubsuit ♣\clubsuit

Having introduced a general theory on the arbor side, it is natural to ask if one can use transmutation in the other direction.

The best hope would be the following statement for every arbor tt:

There should exist a simple polytope Φt\Phi_{t}, some way to orient its skeleton to find the Hasse diagram of a congruence-uniform “Cambrian-like” lattice Λt\Lambda_{t} and some “noncrossing-like” lattice 𝖭𝖢t\mathsf{NC}_{t} built from Λt\Lambda_{t} by the “core-label-order” construction. The lattice 𝖭𝖢t\mathsf{NC}_{t} should be a transmuted partner of PtP_{t}. If the arbor tt has size nn and the poset PtP_{t} has NN elements, then Φt\Phi_{t} should be a simple polytope of dimension nn with NN vertices.

There is so far no idea on how to achieve that in general. A proposal for unary-binary arbors is made in Section 5 in terms of gentle algebras.

A much weaker statement would be to produce starting from tt the simple polytope Φt\Phi_{t} together with a distinguished vertex (as in the top box) whose FF-triangle can be transformed by formulas in Appendix A into an MM-triangle (as in the bottom box) that would be the transmutation of the MM-triangle of PtP_{t}. In particular, Proposition 4.1 says that the hh-vector of tt is then the diagonal of the MM-triangle of the lattice 𝖭𝖢t\mathsf{NC}_{t}, hence describes the grading of this poset and also the hh-vector of the polytope Φt\Phi_{t}.

Again, there is no known idea on how to do that. Two proposals are made in Section 8 and Section 9 that should relate in this way some arbors with known families of polytopes. The evidence is given by a coincidence of hh-vectors, which would follow from the expected transmutation of MM-triangles.

Assuming that we can produce the polytope Φt\Phi_{t} endowed with its distinguished vertex, one could then consider the simplicial complex defined as the dual of the simple polytope Φt\Phi_{t}. One expects that this simplicial complex is flag, and moreover that its Gamma-triangle with respect to the distinguished facet, as defined in [Cha20a], is nonnegative. This holds for all arbors of size at most 1313.

Even weaker is the following conjecture, keeping only minimal information.

Conjecture 0.1.

For every arbor tt, there exists a simple polytope Φt\Phi_{t} such that the hh-vector of tt is equal to the hh-vector of Φt\Phi_{t}.

0.2 Further remarks

The posets that we attach to arbors of type 𝔸\mathbb{A} are special cases of the avalanche posets introduced by Combe and Giraudo in [CG20, CG22]. Despite their very simple nature and the fact that their cardinality is a Catalan number, they do not seem to have been studied much.

The polytopes that we attach to arbors of type 𝔸\mathbb{A} have Catalan-many lattice points. They in fact coincide with a special case of the Pitman-Stanley polytopes introduced in [SP02], when all parameters in the definition are set to 11.

Our notion of pairs of posets being transmuted partners seems to have some relationship, still to be clarified, with the notion of Whitney duality introduced in [GDH21]. Whitney duality relates pairs of posets that exchange their Whitney polynomials of the first and second kind. Some examples involve noncrossing partition lattices. One can in particular note the intriguing fact that the subposet of the poset NCDyck4\operatorname{NCDyck}_{4} of [GDH21, Fig. 9] defined by restriction to indices in the order 1,2,3,41,2,3,4 is isomorphic to the poset PtP_{t} for the arbor of type 𝔸\mathbb{A} on 33 elements.

Note that our notion of arbor has been considered in the literature under various names, including “multilabelled trees” and “rooted trees of non-empty sets” [MSS99, BOS05].

In our examples of transmuted partners, we observe more properties, for example the leading coefficients of the qq-Zeta polynomials [Cha24] are reciprocal of each other as polynomials in qq.

1 Notations and basic properties

Let us start by describing our main combinatorial objects, using the language of species. For an introduction to the theory of species, see [BLL98].

Let SS be the species of sets and S≥1S_{\geq 1} be the species of non-empty sets. Let us consider the species AA defined by the implicit equation

A=S≥1×S⁡(A).A=S_{\geq 1}\times S(A).

In words, this means that the AA-structures on a finite set II are rooted trees, whose vertices are labeled by pairwise disjoint non-empty subsets of II, and the full set of labels is II.

Such a rooted tree will be called an arbor on the set II. For example, here is an arbor on the set {a,b,c,d,e,f}\{a,b,c,d,e,f\}:

.

This example will be used as a running example.

Arbors will either be depicted with their root vertex on the top and growing down as above, or with their root vertex on the left and growing right. The cardinality of a vertex vv will be denoted |v||v|. If |v|≥2|v|\geq 2, then the vertex vv is multiple. The root vertex of an arbor tt will be denoted rtr_{t}.

For a vertex vv of an arbor tt, any vertex ww such that the unique path in tt from ww to the root vertex rtr_{t} passes through vv is called a descendant of vv. This condition is denoted by v⪯wv\preceq w. The set of all descendants of vv form the sub-tree rooted at vv.

To every vertex vv of an arbor, one associates the union of all labels that appear in some descendant of vv. This set is denoted 𝒟⁡(v)\mathscr{D}(v), standing for “down”. In the running example, the sets 𝒟⁡(v)\mathscr{D}(v) are {a,b,c,d,e,f}\{a,b,c,d,e,f\}, {b,e}\{b,e\}, {d}\{d\} and {c}\{c\}.

When |I|=n|I|=n, the arbor tt has size nn.

To every arbor tt on a set II, we will associate both a partial order and a polytope, closely related to each other. Let us start with the polytope.

The ambient space is the vector space over ℝ\mathbb{R} with coordinates (xi)i∈I{(x_{i})}_{i\in I}. The polytope QtQ_{t} is defined by the inequalities 0≤xi0\leq x_{i} for every i∈Ii\in I and

∑i∈𝒟⁡(v)xi≤|𝒟⁡(v)|\sum_{i\in\mathscr{D}(v)}x_{i}\leq|\mathscr{D}(v)| (1)

for every vertex vv. In particular, the inequality attached to the root vertex rtr_{t} says that the sum of all coordinates is less than or equal to |I||I|, so that this indeed defines a bounded polyhedron.

In the running example, besides all coordinates being nonnegative, the defining inequalities are:

xc≤1,xd≤1,xb+xe≤2,xa+xb+xc+xd+xe+xf≤6.x_{c}\leq 1,\quad x_{d}\leq 1,\quad x_{b}+x_{e}\leq 2,\quad x_{a}+x_{b}+x_{c}+x_{d}+x_{e}+x_{f}\leq 6.

The following property is clear from the definition.

Lemma 1.1.

Points with all coordinates in the interval [0,1][0,1] are contained in QtQ_{t}. In other words, the polytope QtQ_{t} contains the standard hypercube.

The definition of polytopes QtQ_{t} by inequalities implies clearly that they are anti-blocking polytopes, in the sense of Fulkerson [Ful71], see also [Sch98, §9.3].

We will often use the height function ht\operatorname{ht} which is the sum of coordinates. Note that the height function is bounded above by |I||I|, which is attained at the point (1,1,…,1)(1,1,\ldots,1).

Let now tt be an arbor on a set of cardinality n≥1n\geq 1. Let (t1,…,t𝗐)(t_{1},\ldots,t_{\mathsf{w}}) be the sub-trees of the root vertex of tt. Let rr be the size of the root vertex of tt. Then the projection π\pi along the coordinates in the root vertex to the other coordinates defines a map from QtQ_{t} to the product ∏kQtk\prod_{k}Q_{t_{k}}. This projection π\pi is surjective as the fiber over any point of total height hh in ∏kQtk\prod_{k}Q_{t_{k}} is the intersection of ℝ≥0r\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{r} with the half-space ∑i∈rtxi≤n−h\sum_{i\in r_{t}}x_{i}\leq n-h. Note that the total height on ∏kQtk\prod_{k}Q_{t_{k}} is less than n−rn-r. In particular, the fibers are simplices of strictly positive dimension.

Lemma 1.2.

The polytope QtQ_{t} is a simple lattice polytope.

Proof.

This is true for arbors of size 11, where QtQ_{t} is the segment [0,1][0,1].

Assume that this is known for all arbors with size strictly less than nn. Let π⁡(Qt)\pi(Q_{t}) denote ∏kQtk\prod_{k}Q_{t_{k}}.

Let zz be a vertex of QtQ_{t}. The point zz must be an extremal point in the fiber π−1​(π​(z))\pi^{-1}(\pi(z)). So its coordinates with indices in the root vertex rtr_{t} are either all 00 or exactly one of them is not 00 and equal to n−hn-h, where hh is the height of π⁡(z)\pi(z). If these coordinates are all 00, then π⁡(z)\pi(z) must be a vertex of ∏kQtk\prod_{k}Q_{t_{k}}. In this case, we obtain a simple vertex with integer coordinates by induction hypothesis.

In the case of exactly one non-zero coordinate, write z=(π⁡(z),n−h,0,…,0)z=(\pi(z),n-h,0,\ldots,0) in the coordinate system where indices in the root come last. Let us show that the point π⁡(z)\pi(z) must still be a vertex of π⁡(Qt)\pi(Q_{t}). Assume by contradiction that π⁡(z)\pi(z) is not extremal. Then there exist distinct z¯1\bar{z}_{1} and z¯2\bar{z}_{2} in π⁡(Qt)\pi(Q_{t}) whose middle is π⁡(z)\pi(z). Let h1h_{1}, h2h_{2} be the heights of z¯1\bar{z}_{1} and z¯2\bar{z}_{2}. Then the height hh of π⁡(z)\pi(z) is (h1+h2)/2(h_{1}+h_{2})/2. Let z1=(z¯1,n−h1,0,…,0)z_{1}=(\bar{z}_{1},n-h_{1},0,\ldots,0) and z2=(z¯2,n−h2,0,…,0)z_{2}=(\bar{z}_{2},n-h_{2},0,\ldots,0) in the same coordinate system. Then both z1z_{1} and z2z_{2} are in QtQ_{t}, distinct, and their middle is zz. Therefore zz is not extremal, which is absurd. Hence π⁡(z)\pi(z) is a vertex of π⁡(Qt)\pi(Q_{t}) and it has integer coordinates and integer height hh by induction. Therefore zz also has integer coordinates.

It follows that there are r+1r+1 vertices of QtQ_{t} in the fiber over each vertex of π⁡(Qt)\pi(Q_{t}). They all have integer coordinates. From the description above, one can also deduce that they are simple. ∎

One can extract from the proof above a recursive description of the vertices of QtQ_{t} themselves. Let us call defect of a point zz in QtQ_{t} at a vertex vv the difference

δv​(z)=|𝒟⁡(v)|−∑i∈𝒟⁡(v)xi​(z)≥0.\delta_{v}(z)=|\mathscr{D}(v)|-\sum_{i\in\mathscr{D}(v)}x_{i}(z)\geq 0. (2)
Lemma 1.3.

For each vertex vv of the arbor tt and for every vertex zz of the polytope QtQ_{t},

  • •

    either all coordinates xi​(z)x_{i}(z) with i∈vi\in v vanish,

  • •

    or exactly one coordinate xi​(z)x_{i}(z) with i∈vi\in v does not vanish.

At every vertex vv where all coordinates vanish, the defect δv​(z)\delta_{v}(z) is at least |v||v|. At every vertex vv where one coordinate is non-zero, the defect δv​(z)\delta_{v}(z) must vanish.

This implies that, assuming all coordinates of a vertex zz of QtQ_{t} for descendant vertices of a vertex vv of tt are fixed, the unique possible non-zero value in the vertex vv is therefore determined by the zero-defect condition, which means that the defining inequality (1) associated with vv must be an equality.

Lemma 1.4.

The polytope QtQ_{t} has no interior lattice point.

Proof.

Every interior lattice point must have all coordinates xi>0x_{i}>0, but the sum of coordinates must be an integer strictly less than |I||I|. ∎

Let us now define the poset PtP_{t}. The elements of PtP_{t} are the lattice points of QtQ_{t}. The partial order is defined by comparison of coordinates, namely x≤yx\leq y if and only if xi≤yix_{i}\leq y_{i} for all i∈Ii\in I. The poset PtP_{t} has a unique minimum 00 and is graded by the height function ht\operatorname{ht}.

From the definition of PtP_{t}, one deduces the following property.

Lemma 1.5.

For every element aa in PtP_{t}, the interval [0,a][0,a] is a product of total orders whose lengths are the non-zero coordinates of aa plus one.

This property implies that one can consider the Hasse diagram as the skeleton of a cubical complex, by glueing together the cubical complexes for products of total orders.

In the running example, the polytope QtQ_{t} is a 66-dimensional simple lattice polytope with ff-vector (36,108,141,102,43,10,1)(36,108,141,102,43,10,1). The poset PtP_{t} has 330330 elements, which are the lattice points of QtQ_{t}. The cubical complex of PtP_{t} has ff-vector (330,990,1152,654,186,24,1)(330,990,1152,654,186,24,1). A simpler example is illustrated in Figure 1.

Note that both the polytope QtQ_{t} and the poset PtP_{t} are species, in the sense that every bijection I≃JI\simeq J that induces a relabeling of tt also induces an isomorphism of polytopes and posets. We will from now on work with isomorphism classes of arbors.

1.1 Minkowski decomposition

Let tt be an arbor on the set II. Let us show that the polytope QtQ_{t} admits a nice decomposition as a Minkowski sum of simplices.

Let us first describe the Minkowski summands. There will be a summand UvU_{v} associated with every vertex vv of tt.

For every vertex vv, define a subset 𝒰⁡(v)\mathscr{U}(v) of II, standing for “up”, as the union of the sets attached to all vertices of tt in the unique path in tt from the root rtr_{t} of tt to the vertex vv. The polytope UvU_{v} is the convex hull inside ℝ𝒰⁡(v)\mathbb{R}^{\mathscr{U}(v)} of the origin and all |v|​ei|v|e_{i} where eie_{i} are the basis vectors of ℝ𝒰⁡(v)\mathbb{R}^{\mathscr{U}(v)}. Note that it is a Minkowski multiple of the basic simplex whose vertices are the origin and the eie_{i}.

In the running example, the subsets 𝒰⁡(v)\mathscr{U}(v) are {a,f},{a,f,b,e},{a,f,d}\{a,f\},\{a,f,b,e\},\{a,f,d\} and {a,f,c}\{a,f,c\}.

Let

𝕄t=∑vUv\mathbb{M}_{t}=\sum_{v}U_{v} (3)

be the Minkowski sum of these simplices. We will show that 𝕄t=Qt\mathbb{M}_{t}=Q_{t} by inclusion in both directions.

Lemma 1.6.

Every point in 𝕄t\mathbb{M}_{t} satisfies all the defining inequalities of QtQ_{t}.

Proof.

This is clear for the inequalities xi≥0x_{i}\geq 0 for i∈Ii\in I, because all Minkowski summands UvU_{v} have nonnegative coordinates. So let us consider the inequality attached to a vertex vv of tt. Fix an element ee in the Minkowski sum 𝕄t\mathbb{M}_{t}, written as

e=∑wew,e=\sum_{w}e_{w},

where ew∈Uwe_{w}\in U_{w}. The inequality to check is

∑i∈𝒟⁡(v)xi​(e)≤|𝒟⁡(v)|.\sum_{i\in\mathscr{D}(v)}x_{i}(e)\leq|\mathscr{D}(v)|.

So we need to bound the sum

∑i∈𝒟⁡(v)∑wxi​(ew).\sum_{i\in\mathscr{D}(v)}\sum_{w}x_{i}(e_{w}).

When ww is not a descendant of vv, the Minkowski summand UwU_{w} involves only coordinates in 𝒰⁡(w)\mathscr{U}(w) which is disjoint from 𝒟⁡(v)\mathscr{D}(v). Therefore the sum above can be restricted to ww in the set of descendants of vv:

∑v⪯w∑i∈𝒟⁡(v)∩𝒰⁡(w)xi​(ew).\sum_{v\preceq w}\sum_{i\in\mathscr{D}(v)\cap\mathscr{U}(w)}x_{i}(e_{w}).

By definition, the summand UwU_{w} is a dilated basic simplex, hence

∑i∈𝒰⁡(w)xi​(ew)≤|w|.\sum_{i\in\mathscr{U}(w)}x_{i}(e_{w})\leq|w|.

Therefore our full sum is bounded above by

∑v⪯w|w|=|𝒟⁡(v)|.\sum_{v\preceq w}|w|=|\mathscr{D}(v)|.

∎

Lemma 1.7.

Let tt be an arbor on the set II. Every vertex of the polytope QtQ_{t} belongs to 𝕄t\mathbb{M}_{t}.

The proof is done by induction on the size of the arbor. This clearly holds for arbors with just one vertex. The proof will use the recursive description of vertices given in Lemma 1.3 and the defects.

Proof.

Let (t1,…,t𝗐)(t_{1},\ldots,t_{\mathsf{w}}) be the sub-trees of the root vertex rtr_{t} of tt. Let zz be a vertex of QtQ_{t}. By induction on the size of tt, the statement holds for all sub-trees tkt_{k}. As the image of π\pi is the direct product of the polytopes QtkQ_{t_{k}}, one can take the direct product of the Minkowski decompositions of QtkQ_{t_{k}}. Therefore the image π⁡(z)\pi(z) can be written as a sum

π⁡(z)=∑w≠rtew,\pi(z)=\sum_{w\not=r_{t}}e_{w}, (4)

where ewe_{w} is in the Minkowski summand UwU_{w} for some vertex ww in some tkt_{k}.

If all coordinates xi​(z)x_{i}(z) for i∈rti\in r_{t} vanish, then to each ewe_{w} in the sum (4) one can associate a point fwf_{w} with the same coordinates plus additional zero coordinates for all vertices i∈rti\in r_{t}. This defines a point fwf_{w} in the summand UwU_{w} of 𝕄t\mathbb{M}_{t}, as the sum of coordinates in 𝒰⁡(w)\mathscr{U}(w) is unchanged. The sum ∑w≠rtfw\sum_{w\not=r_{t}}f_{w} is therefore in 𝕄t\mathbb{M}_{t} and coincides with zz by construction.

Assume now that exactly one coordinate xi​(z)x_{i}(z) with i∈rti\in r_{t} is non-zero. Because the defect δrt​(z)\delta_{r_{t}}(z) vanishes, one gets

xi​(z)+∑j∉rtxj​(z)=n=|rt|+∑k∑w∈tk|w|.x_{i}(z)+\sum_{j\not\in r_{t}}x_{j}(z)=n=|r_{t}|+\sum_{k}\sum_{w\in t_{k}}|w|.

It follows that

xi​(z)−|rt|=∑kδk​(z),x_{i}(z)-|r_{t}|=\sum_{k}\delta_{k}(z), (5)

where δk​(z)\delta_{k}(z) is the defect of zz with respect to the root vertex of tkt_{k}.

Consider the set SS of vertices that can be reached from the root rtr_{t} by repeatedly moving to the root ww of a sub-tree with non-zero defect δw​(z)\delta_{w}(z). Let ww be a vertex in SS. Then from the element ewe_{w} in the summand UwU_{w} of some 𝕄tk\mathbb{M}_{t_{k}}, define fwf_{w} by adding a new coordinate xix_{i} with value |w||w| plus other zero coordinates for other vertices j∈rtj\in r_{t}.

Let us check that fwf_{w} is an element in the summand UwU_{w} of 𝕄t\mathbb{M}_{t}. Certainly all coordinates of fwf_{w} are nonnegative. Because the defect δv​(z)\delta_{v}(z) is not zero for every vertex v≠rtv\not=r_{t} on the path between rtr_{t} and ww, all coordinates xj​(z)x_{j}(z) with jj in 𝒰⁡(w)∖rt\mathscr{U}(w)\setminus r_{t} are zero. The sum of all coordinates of fwf_{w} is therefore |w||w|. It follows that fwf_{w} is in the summand UwU_{w} of 𝕄t\mathbb{M}_{t}.

Let us consider z′=∑w≠rtfwz^{\prime}=\sum_{w\not=r_{t}}f_{w}. Then for all j∉rj\not\in r, the coordinates xj​(z)x_{j}(z) and xj​(z′)x_{j}(z^{\prime}) coincide by construction. For j∈rtj\in r_{t} not equal to ii, the coordinates xj​(z)x_{j}(z) and xj​(z′)x_{j}(z^{\prime}) both vanish. Only the coordinate xix_{i} may differ between zz and z′z^{\prime}. By construction xi​(z′)x_{i}(z^{\prime}) is the sum of |w||w| over all vertices ww in the reachable set SS.

Let us prove that this sum over SS is equal to xi​(z)−|rt|x_{i}(z)-|r_{t}|. Let us start with (5) or more precisely its restriction to sub-trees tkt_{k} whose root has non-zero defect. For every such kk, the defect δk​(z)\delta_{k}(z) is the sum of the size of the root of tkt_{k} plus the sum of the defects of the roots of sub-trees of tkt_{k}. Iterating this process over the set SS, one obtains the expected equality:

xi​(z)−|rt|=∑w∈S|w|.x_{i}(z)-|r_{t}|=\sum_{w\in S}|w|.

Let then frtf_{r_{t}} be the element of the summand UrtU_{r_{t}} with coordinate ii equal to |rt||r_{t}| and other coordinates 00. Then z′+frt=zz^{\prime}+f_{r_{t}}=z, and therefore z∈𝕄tz\in\mathbb{M}_{t}. ∎

One can use this Minkowski decomposition to define a canonical polynomial whose Newton polytope is QtQ_{t}, namely

∏v(1+∑e∈𝒰⁡(v)xe)|v|.\prod_{v}{\left(1+\sum_{e\in\mathscr{U}(v)}x_{e}\right)}^{|v|}. (6)

In the case of the arbors of type 𝔸\mathbb{A}, namely linear arbors with no multiple vertex, these polynomials have appeared in the literature in relation with Catalan numbers. They are item 210 in Stanley’s book [Sta15]. According to the errata of this book, these polynomials first appeared in 1982 in a problem by J. Shallit in [Sha82, SW86]. They have been studied recently in [Fri21].

Let us state a corollary of the Minkowski decomposition. Postnikov introduced in [Pos09] the notion of YY-generalized permutohedra, defined as Minkowski sums of scaled standard simplices.

Let e0,e1,…,ede_{0},e_{1},\ldots,e_{d} denote the standard basis of ℤd+1\mathbb{Z}^{d+1}. A scaled standard simplex is the convex hull of a set of vectors {ki​ei}i∈I{\{k_{i}e_{i}\}}_{i\in I} where II is a non-empty subset of {0,1,…,d}\{0,1,\ldots,d\} and kik_{i} are positive integers.

Lemma 1.8.

The polytope QtQ_{t} is, up to unimodular equivalence, a YY-generalized permutohedra.

Proof.

Let us consider the finest Minkowski decomposition of QtQ_{t}, where each summand UvU_{v} is further decomposed as a Minkowski sum of equal terms. In this decomposition, each summand is the convex hull in ℤd\mathbb{Z}^{d} of 00 and some vectors {ei}i∈I{\{e_{i}\}}_{i\in I} where II is a non-empty subset of {1,…,d}\{1,\ldots,d\}. This defines a polytope ΔI\Delta_{I} in ℤd\mathbb{Z}^{d}, to which one associates a standard simplex ΔI′\Delta^{\prime}_{I} in ℤd+1\mathbb{Z}^{d+1} by replacing the vertex 00 by the basis vector e0e_{0}. Let us consider the linear map ρ\rho from ℤd+1\mathbb{Z}^{d+1} to ℤd\mathbb{Z}^{d} that forgets the first coordinate. Then ρ\rho maps ΔI′\Delta^{\prime}_{I} to ΔI\Delta_{I} and is moreover a unimodular equivalence from ΔI′\Delta^{\prime}_{I} to ΔI\Delta_{I}.

Let us write Qt=∑s∈SΔIsQ_{t}=\sum_{s\in S}\Delta_{I_{s}} and Qt′=∑s∈SΔIs′Q^{\prime}_{t}=\sum_{s\in S}\Delta^{\prime}_{I_{s}} over the appropriate indexing set SS. Then ρ\rho induces an invertible integral affine map from the hyperplane HH in ℤd+1\mathbb{Z}^{d+1} where coordinates sum to |S||S| to ℤd\mathbb{Z}^{d}, that maps Qt′Q^{\prime}_{t} to QtQ_{t}. This is the expected unimodular equivalence. ∎

2 Invariants

We will be interested in several invariants of the polytope QtQ_{t} and the poset PtP_{t}. Let us explain how they can be computed by induction.

The basis of the inductions is always the unique isomorphism class of arbor on a set with one element. The polytope QtQ_{t} is in this case the line segment [0,1][0,1] in ℝ\mathbb{R} and the poset PtP_{t} is a total order with 22 elements.

The induction steps will use the following property or some variation of it, that come from the surjective projection map π\pi described in Section 1. Let tt be an arbor and t1,…,t𝗐t_{1},\ldots,t_{\mathsf{w}} be the sub-trees of the root vertex of tt. If ee is a lattice point in QtQ_{t}, then one can describe ee using one lattice point eke_{k} in QtkQ_{t_{k}} for every 1≤k≤𝗐1\leq k\leq\mathsf{w} by restriction, plus the additional data of the coordinates of ee with indices in the root vertex. The only constraint on these root coordinates is their sum, namely the height of ee has to be the sum of the heights of all eke_{k} plus the sum of the root coordinates. The same statement holds for all real points.

2.1 Ehrhart polynomial

Let us first consider the Ehrhart polynomial EtE_{t} of the lattice polytope QtQ_{t}. Recall that this is the unique polynomial EtE_{t} in a variable uu such that, for every integer m≥1m\geq 1, Et​(m)E_{t}(m) is the number of lattice points in the dilated polytope m​QtmQ_{t}. A standard reference on the subject is [Bar08].

In order to compute the Ehrhart polynomial, we will need to refine the count according to height. This is done in a somewhat indirect way, maybe not optimal.

For every integer m≥1m\geq 1, let us introduce a polynomial Ft,mF_{t,m} in the variable XX that counts lattice points in the dilated polytope m​QtmQ_{t} with weight XhX^{h} at height hh. For an arbor of size nn, the height on m​QtmQ_{t} is bounded above by m​nmn, so Ft,mF_{t,m} has degree m​nmn.

Note that this definition of Ft,mF_{t,m} could be extended verbatim to any lattice polytope in ℝ≥0n\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{n}. In this generality, it is clearly multiplicative with respect to direct product of polytopes.

For the arbor tt on one element,

Ft,m=1+X+⋯+Xm.F_{t,m}=1+X+\cdots+X^{m}. (7)

Let tt be an arbor on a set of cardinality n≥2n\geq 2. Let (t1,…,t𝗐)(t_{1},\ldots,t_{\mathsf{w}}) be the sub-trees of the root vertex of tt. Let rr be the size of the root vertex of tt.

Proposition 2.1.

Let m≥1m\geq 1 be an integer. Let FW,mF_{W,m} be the product ∏k=1𝗐Ftk,m\prod_{k=1}^{\mathsf{w}}F_{t_{k},m}. Write FW,m=∑jWj​XjF_{W,m}=\sum_{j}W_{j}X^{j}. Then for 0≤j≤m​n0\leq j\leq mn, the coefficient of XjX^{j} in Ft,mF_{t,m} is

∑ℓ=max⁡(0,j+m⁡(r−n))j(r+ℓ−1ℓ)​Wj−ℓ.\sum_{\ell=\max(0,j+m(r-n))}^{j}\binom{r+\ell-1}{\ell}W_{j-\ell}. (8)
Proof.

Let us fix an integer mm and consider the dilated polytope m​QtmQ_{t}.

For 0≤j≤m​n0\leq j\leq mn, a point at height jj in m​QtmQ_{t} can be described by the coordinates of its image by the projection map π\pi together with the remaining rr coordinates from the root vertex of tt. Assume that the image by π\pi has height j−ℓj-\ell, with 0≤ℓ≤j0\leq\ell\leq j. The possible images are counted by Wj−ℓW_{j-\ell}, which vanishes if j−ℓ>m⁡(n−r)j-\ell>m(n-r) because the degree of Fw,mF_{w,m} is m⁡(n−r)m(n-r). Then the coordinates from the root vertex describe a point in ℕr\mathbb{N}^{r} with height ℓ\ell. This set is well-known to be counted by (r+ℓ−1ℓ)\binom{r+\ell-1}{\ell}.

As this is a bijection, we get the expected sum over ℓ\ell. ∎

This allows to compute the usual Ehrhart polynomial by interpolation of the values of Ft,mF_{t,m} at X=1X=1 with respect to mm.

For the running example, one finds that EtE_{t} is

112⋅(2​u+1)⋅(u+1)3⋅(83​u2+70​u+12),\frac{1}{12}\cdot(2u+1)\cdot{(u+1)}^{3}\cdot(83u^{2}+70u+12),

and so the volume is the leading coefficient 83/683/6.

Conjecture 2.2.

For any arbor tt, all roots of the Ehrhart polynomial of QtQ_{t} are negative real numbers in the interval [−1,0][-1,0], excluding 00.

Indeed 00 is not a root because the constant term is always 11. This conjecture has been checked for all arbors of size at most 1212.

Note that this conjecture would imply that all coefficients of the Ehrhart polynomial are positive. A lattice polytope with this property is said to be Ehrhart positive. Postnikov proved in [Pos09] that all YY-generalized permutohedra are Ehrhart positive, see also [Liu19, §3.1] and [FH23, §6.1]. By lemma 1.8, one can conclude that the polytope QtQ_{t} is Ehrhart positive.

2.2 Volume

Let us now consider the volume of the polytope QtQ_{t}. This could be computed using the leading coefficient of the Ehrhart polynomial. Instead, we refine here the volume into a volume function Vt​(h)V_{t}(h), that records the volume of every slice of QtQ_{t} according to the height function ht\operatorname{ht}. This function vanishes outside the segment [0,n][0,n] where nn is the size of tt.

This volume-function could be defined verbatim for any polytope in ℝ≥0n\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{n}. In this generality, the volume-function of a direct product of polytopes is the convolution of the individual volume-functions.

For the arbor tt on one element,

Vt​(h)=1,V_{t}(h)=1, (9)

for 0≤h≤10\leq h\leq 1 and 00 otherwise.

Let tt be an arbor on a set of cardinality n≥2n\geq 2. Let (t1,…,t𝗐)(t_{1},\ldots,t_{\mathsf{w}}) be the sub-trees of the root vertex of tt. Let rr be the size of the root vertex of tt.

Let ⋆\star denote the convolution product of functions on ℝ≥0\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}. Let 𝖳n\mathsf{T}_{n} denote the operator that truncates a function to the segment [0,n][0,n], extended by zero outside of this segment.

Proposition 2.3.

The volume function VtV_{t} is given by

𝖳n(Vt1⋆Vt2⋆⋯⋆Vt𝗐⋆Wn,r),\mathsf{T}_{n}(V_{t_{1}}\star V_{t_{2}}\star\cdots\star V_{t_{\mathsf{w}}}\star W_{n,r}), (10)

where Wn,rW_{n,r} is the truncated function 𝖳n​(hr−1(r−1)!)\mathsf{T}_{n}\left(\frac{h^{r-1}}{(r-1)!}\right).

Proof.

Recall that a point in QtQ_{t} is determined by a sequence of points eke_{k} in QtkQ_{t_{k}} by restriction and by a point in ℝr\mathbb{R}^{r} for the coordinates with indices in the root vertex of tt. The additional constraint is the value of the height. Using multiplicativity, one checks that the volume of a slice in QtQ_{t} is the expected convolution, except maybe for heights above nn. This is fixed by the truncation operator wrapping the convolution products. ∎

The volume function allows to compute the volume by integration from 00 to nn. This matches the leading coefficient of the Ehrhart polynomial.

In general, the function VtV_{t} is continuous and piecewise-polynomial with possible change of polynomial at integers. In the running example for instance, it is given by h5/120h^{5}/120 between 00 and 11, by three complicated polynomials of degree 55 between 11 and 44 and by 2​h−14/32h-14/3 between 44 and 66. Integrating from 00 to 66, one computes the volume to be 83/683/6 as expected.

2.3 Laplace transform of volume

The volume function VtV_{t} is in general a rather complicated piecewise-polynomial function of the variable hh. It is more compactly encoded by its Laplace transform, defined by

Lt​(v)=∫0∞e−v​h​Vt​(h)​𝑑h.L_{t}(v)=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-vh}V_{t}(h)dh. (11)

Note that the value at v=0v=0 recovers the volume of QtQ_{t}.

The Laplace transform sends the convolution product to the product. It therefore remains to understand the truncation operator 𝖳n\mathsf{T}_{n} after the transform. We will only need the action of 𝖳n\mathsf{T}_{n} on the functions ek,ℓ​(v)=v−k​e−ℓ​ve_{k,\ell}(v)=v^{-k}e^{-\ell v} with k>0k>0 and ℓ≥0\ell\geq 0.

Lemma 2.4.

For integers k≥0k\geq 0 and ℓ≥0\ell\geq 0, let fk,ℓf_{k,\ell} be the function on ℝ≥0\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} defined by (h−ℓ)kk!\frac{{(h-\ell)}^{k}}{k!} if h>ℓh>\ell and 00 otherwise. The Laplace transform of fk,ℓf_{k,\ell} is v−k−1​e−ℓ​vv^{-k-1}e^{-\ell v}.

This statement is easy to prove by standard properties of the Laplace transform, see [DLMF, Table 1.14.4].

Lemma 2.5.

If ℓ≥n\ell\geq n, then 𝖳n​(ek,ℓ)=0\mathsf{T}_{n}(e_{k,\ell})=0. Otherwise

𝖳n​(ek+1,ℓ)=ek+1,ℓ−∑j=0k(n−ℓ)k−j(k−j)!​ej+1,n.\mathsf{T}_{n}(e_{k+1,\ell})=e_{k+1,\ell}-\sum_{j=0}^{k}\frac{{(n-\ell)}^{k-j}}{(k-j)!}e_{j+1,n}. (12)
Proof.

Let gn​(h)g_{n}(h) be the indicatrix function of the interval [0,n][0,n]. As gn=f0,0−f0,ng_{n}=f_{0,0}-f_{0,n}, its Laplace transform is ℒ​gn=1v​(1−e−n​v)\mathcal{L}g_{n}=\frac{1}{v}(1-e^{-nv}). The truncation operator acts on functions of hh as the pointwise product with gng_{n}. Because fk,ℓf_{k,\ell} has support on [ℓ,∞][\ell,\infty], this pointwise product fk,ℓ​gnf_{k,\ell}g_{n} is the zero function if ℓ≥n\ell\geq n. So 𝖳n​(ek,ℓ)\mathsf{T}_{n}(e_{k,\ell}) is zero in this case.

Otherwise, assume ℓ<n\ell<n. Let us start from

fk,ℓ​gn=fk,ℓ−f0,n​fk,ℓf_{k,\ell}g_{n}=f_{k,\ell}-f_{0,n}f_{k,\ell}

and compute the Laplace transform:

e−ℓ​vvk+1−∫n∞(h−ℓ)kk!​e−v​h​𝑑h.\frac{e^{-\ell v}}{v^{k+1}}-\int_{n}^{\infty}\frac{{(h-\ell)}^{k}}{k!}e^{-vh}dh.

The second term becomes, first replacing h−ℓh-\ell by (h−n)+(n−ℓ)(h-n)+(n-\ell) and expanding,

∑j=0k(n−ℓ)k−j(k−j)!​e−n​vvj+1.\sum_{j=0}^{k}\frac{{(n-\ell)}^{k-j}}{(k-j)!}\frac{e^{-nv}}{v^{j+1}}.

This proves the expected formula. ∎

One can therefore compute the Laplace transform Lt​(v)L_{t}(v) of the volume function VtV_{t} by first computing by induction a polynomial Lt​(E,V)L_{t}(E,V) in variables EE and VV using the following rules, and then replace EE by e−ve^{-v} and VV by 1/v1/v.

The initial value Lt​(E,V)L_{t}(E,V) for the arbor of size 11 is −V​E+V-VE+V.

The truncation formula (12) translates into a similar formula for the action of 𝖳n\mathsf{T}_{n} on polynomials in EE and VV.

Let tt be an arbor on a set of cardinality n≥2n\geq 2. Let (t1,…,t𝗐)(t_{1},\ldots,t_{\mathsf{w}}) be the sub-trees of the root vertex of tt. Let rr be the size of the root vertex of tt.

Proposition 2.6.

The polynomial Lt​(E,V)L_{t}(E,V) is 𝖳n​(∏k=1𝗐Ltk​(E,V)⋅𝖳n​(Vr))\mathsf{T}_{n}(\prod_{k=1}^{\mathsf{w}}L_{t_{k}}(E,V)\cdot\mathsf{T}_{n}(V^{r})).

Proof.

This follows from the preceding statements. The function Wn,rW_{n,r} has Laplace transform equal to 𝖳n​(v−r)\mathsf{T}_{n}\left(v^{-r}\right) by Lemma 2.4. ∎

In the running example, this gives

−V6​E4+2​V6​E3−2​V5​E4+4​V5​E3−2​V2​E6−2​V6​E−2​V5​E2−223​V​E6+V6.-V^{6}E^{4}+2V^{6}E^{3}-2V^{5}E^{4}+4V^{5}E^{3}-2V^{2}E^{6}-2V^{6}E-2V^{5}E^{2}-\frac{22}{3}VE^{6}+V^{6}.

To recover the volume, one needs to take the limit at v=0v=0 of Lt​(e−v,1/v)L_{t}(e^{-v},1/v).

2.4 Zeta polynomial

Let us now consider the Zeta polynomial of the poset PtP_{t}. This is a polynomial ZtZ_{t} in the variable uu whose value at every integer m≥2m\geq 2 is the number of chains e1≤e2≤⋯≤em−1e_{1}\leq e_{2}\leq\cdots\leq e_{m-1} in PtP_{t}.

We will need a mild refinement of this usual Zeta polynomial. Let 𝖹t​(u,X)\mathsf{Z}_{t}(u,X) be the polynomial in uu and XX such that for every integer m≥2m\geq 2,

𝖹t​(m,X)=∑e1≤⋯≤em−1Xht⁡(em−1)\mathsf{Z}_{t}(m,X)=\sum_{e_{1}\leq\cdots\leq e_{m-1}}X^{\operatorname{ht}(e_{m-1})} (13)

where ht\operatorname{ht} is the height of an element. The existence of this polynomial will follow from the induction below. Setting X=1X=1 forgets about the height and gives the usual Zeta polynomial.

Note that if we consider a product of two graded posets endowed with the sum of height functions, then the definition of 𝖹\mathsf{Z} is naturally multiplicative, as chains are then just pairs of chains of the same length.

For the arbor tt on one element, one finds that

𝖹t​(u,X)=1+(u−1)​X.\mathsf{Z}_{t}(u,X)=1+(u-1)X. (14)

Let now tt be an arbor on a set of cardinality n≥2n\geq 2. Let (t1,…,t𝗐)(t_{1},\ldots,t_{\mathsf{w}}) be the sub-trees of the root vertex of tt. Let rr be the size of the root vertex of tt.

Proposition 2.7.

Let 𝖹W\mathsf{Z}_{W} be the product of ∏k=1𝗐𝖹𝗍𝗄\prod_{k=1}^{\mathsf{w}}\mathsf{Z_{t_{k}}}. Write 𝖹W=∑jWj​Xj\mathsf{Z}_{W}=\sum_{j}W_{j}X^{j}. Then for 0≤j≤n0\leq j\leq n, the coefficient of XjX^{j} in 𝖹t\mathsf{Z}_{t} is

∑ℓ=max⁡(0,j−n+r)j(r⁡(u−1)+ℓ−1ℓ)​Wj−ℓ.\sum_{\ell=\max(0,j-n+r)}^{j}\binom{r(u-1)+\ell-1}{\ell}W_{j-\ell}. (15)
Proof.

Let us fix an integer m≥2m\geq 2 and consider a chain e1≤⋯≤em−1e_{1}\leq\cdots\leq e_{m-1} in PtP_{t} with ht⁡(em−1)=j\operatorname{ht}(e_{m-1})=j. Because the interval [0,em−1][0,e_{m-1}] is a product of total orders, one can decompose the chain as a product of chains of the same length by separating the coordinates in two disjoint subsets: AA for those in the root vertex of tt and BB for the others. Let ℓ\ell be the sum of coordinates of em−1e_{m-1} in AA and j−ℓj-\ell be the sum of coordinates of em−1e_{m-1} in BB. Note that j−ℓ≤n−rj-\ell\leq n-r by the defining inequalities for the sub-trees t1,…,t𝗐t_{1},\ldots,t_{\mathsf{w}}.

On the set BB, the restriction of the chain is a product of chains in the sub-trees t1,…,t𝗐t_{1},\ldots,t_{\mathsf{w}} with maximal height j−ℓj-\ell. Such chains are counted by Wj−ℓW_{j-\ell} evaluated at u=mu=m. On the set AA, the restriction of the chain is a chain in the poset ℕr\mathbb{N}^{r} ordered coordinate-wise, with maximal height equal to ℓ\ell. By Theorem 7.2 in Section 7, chains of length m−1m-1 in the poset ℕr\mathbb{N}^{r} with maximal height at most ℓ\ell are counted by (r⁡(m−1)+ℓℓ)\binom{r(m-1)+\ell}{\ell}. Therefore, by taking the difference of values for ℓ\ell and ℓ−1\ell-1, the possible restricted chains on the set AA are counted by (r⁡(m−1)+ℓ−1ℓ)\binom{r(m-1)+\ell-1}{\ell}.

This decomposition is a bijection, hence the expected formula holds for every m≥2m\geq 2. Hence it holds as an equality of polynomials in uu. ∎

In the running example, one gets

𝖹t=190⋅((802​u4−1839​u3+1598​u2−621​u+90)​(2​u−1)​(u−1)​X6CLOSE+6​(53​u2−77​u+30)​(4​u−3)​(2​u−1)​(u−1)​X5+45​(68​u3−156​u2+119​u−30)​(u−1)​X4+60​(11​u−10)​(4​u−3)​(u−1)​X3OPEN+90​(17​u−15)​(u−1)​X2+540​(u−1)​X+90)\mathsf{Z}_{t}=\frac{1}{90}\cdot\Bigl({\left(802\,u^{4}-1839\,u^{3}+1598\,u^{2}-621\,u+90\right)}{\left(2\,u-1\right)}{\left(u-1\right)}X^{6}\\ +6\,{\left(53\,u^{2}-77\,u+30\right)}{\left(4\,u-3\right)}{\left(2\,u-1\right)}{\left(u-1\right)}X^{5}\\ +45\,{\left(68\,u^{3}-156\,u^{2}+119\,u-30\right)}{\left(u-1\right)}X^{4}\\ +60\,{\left(11\,u-10\right)}{\left(4\,u-3\right)}{\left(u-1\right)}X^{3}\\ +90\,{\left(17\,u-15\right)}{\left(u-1\right)}X^{2}+540\,{\left(u-1\right)}X+90\Bigr)

and so the usual Zeta polynomial is

190⋅u⋅(2​u−1)⋅(802​u4−1369​u3+893​u2−266​u+30).\frac{1}{90}\cdot u\cdot(2u-1)\cdot(802u^{4}-1369u^{3}+893u^{2}-266u+30).

It seems that the set of arbors tt having the property that the Zeta polynomial of PtP_{t} factors completely over ℚ\mathbb{Q} consists exactly of arbors of type 𝔸\mathbb{A} considered in Section 6, arbors of type 𝔹\mathbb{B} considered in section Section 7 and one of the two families considered in Section 8.

2.5 MM-triangle

Let us now consider the MM-triangle of the poset PtP_{t}. This is the polynomial Mt​(X,Y)M_{t}(X,Y) defined by (55) in Appendix A, using values of the Möbius function.

In order to give a recursive formula, we need to compute instead the following polynomial

Kt​(X,Y)=∑a∈PtXnz⁡(a)​Yht⁡(a),K_{t}(X,Y)=\sum_{a\in P_{t}}X^{\operatorname{nz}(a)}Y^{\operatorname{ht}(a)}, (16)

where nz⁡(a)\operatorname{nz}(a) is the number of non-zero coordinates in aa. Note that the exponent of XX is smaller than or equal to the exponent of YY in any monomial in this formula.

Note that the polynomial KtK_{t} is clearly multiplicative under product for posets of the type that we are considering.

For the arbor tt on one element,

Kt=1+X​Y.K_{t}=1+XY. (17)

Let tt be an arbor on a set of cardinality n≥2n\geq 2. Let (t1,…,t𝗐)(t_{1},\ldots,t_{\mathsf{w}}) be the sub-trees of the root vertex of tt. Let rr be the size of the root vertex of tt.

Proposition 2.8.

Let W=∏kKtkW=\prod_{k}K_{t_{k}} and write W=∑i,jWi,j​Xi​YjW=\sum_{i,j}W_{i,j}X^{i}Y^{j}. Then for 0≤j≤k≤n0\leq j\leq k\leq n, the coefficient of Xj​YkX^{j}Y^{k} in KtK_{t} is

∑ℓ=max⁡(0,j−n+r)min⁡(j,r)∑m=max⁡(ℓ,k−n+r)k+ℓ−j(rℓ)​(m−1m−ℓ)​Wj−ℓ,k−m.\sum_{\ell=\max(0,j-n+r)}^{\min(j,r)}\sum_{m=\max(\ell,k-n+r)}^{k+\ell-j}\binom{r}{\ell}\binom{m-1}{m-\ell}W_{j-\ell,k-m}. (18)
Proof.

Any element aa of PtP_{t} can be described as an element π⁡(a)\pi(a) of ∏kPtk\prod_{k}P_{t_{k}} and rr additional coordinates from the root of tt for the fiber of π\pi. Let us assume that aa has jj non-zero coordinates and height kk, with 0≤j≤k≤n0\leq j\leq k\leq n. Assume now that π⁡(a)\pi(a) has j−ℓj-\ell non-zero coordinates and height k−mk-m with 0≤ℓ≤j0\leq\ell\leq j and 0≤m≤k0\leq m\leq k. This also requires that 0≤j−ℓ≤k−m≤n−r0\leq j-\ell\leq k-m\leq n-r.

Then the additional rr coordinates must sum to mm and among them exactly ℓ\ell must be non-zero. This implies that ℓ≤r\ell\leq r and ℓ≤m\ell\leq m. The choice of these non-zero coordinates is counted by a binomial (rℓ)\binom{r}{\ell}. Once this choice is fixed, there remains to choose ℓ\ell strictly positive numbers summing to mm, which amounts to choose ℓ−1\ell-1 cuts among m−1m-1 possible inner cuts in a sequence of length mm.

As this defines a bijection, one gets the expected double sum, where the projection π⁡(a)\pi(a) contributes by the term Wj−ℓ,k−mW_{j-\ell,k-m} and the coordinates from the root contribute the product (rℓ)​(m−1m−ℓ)\binom{r}{\ell}\binom{m-1}{m-\ell}. The precise bounds in the double sum follows from the necessary inequalities as previously stated. ∎

Here is a slightly simplified version of Proposition 2.8 that will be useful.

Proposition 2.9.

Let W=∏kKtkW=\prod_{k}K_{t_{k}} and write W=∑i,jWi,j​Xi​YjW=\sum_{i,j}W_{i,j}X^{i}Y^{j}. Then for 0≤j≤n0\leq j\leq n, the coefficient of XjX^{j} in Kt​(X,1)K_{t}(X,1) is

∑ℓ=max⁡(0,j−n+r)min⁡(j,r)∑k′=j−ℓn−r(rℓ)​(n−k′ℓ)​Wj−ℓ,k′.\sum_{\ell=\max(0,j-n+r)}^{\min(j,r)}\sum_{k^{\prime}=j-\ell}^{n-r}\binom{r}{\ell}\binom{n-k^{\prime}}{\ell}W_{j-\ell,k^{\prime}}. (19)
Proof.

Starting from Proposition 2.8 and summing over kk, one gets

∑k,ℓ,m(rℓ)​(m−1m−ℓ)​Wj−ℓ,k−m\sum_{k,\ell,m}\binom{r}{\ell}\binom{m-1}{m-\ell}W_{j-\ell,k-m} (20)

over the appropriate range. By first changing variable to k′=k−mk^{\prime}=k-m, one can perform the inner summation over mm from ℓ\ell to n−k′n-k^{\prime}. ∎

The polynomial KtK_{t} determines the MM-triangle MtM_{t} as follows.

Proposition 2.10.

For every arbor tt,

Mt​(X,Y)=Kt​(1−1/X,X​Y).M_{t}(X,Y)=K_{t}(1-1/X,XY). (21)
Proof.

First, write the MM-triangle as a double sum

∑b∈PtYht⁡(b)​∑a≤bμ⁡(a,b)​Xht⁡(a).\sum_{b\in P_{t}}Y^{\operatorname{ht}(b)}\sum_{a\leq b}\mu(a,b)X^{\operatorname{ht}(a)}.

Recall that the interval [0,b][0,b] is a product of total orders whose lengths are the non-zero coordinates of bb plus 11. It follows that the inner sum is

∑a≤bμ⁡(a,b)​Xht⁡(a)=Xht⁡(b)​(1−1/X)nz⁡(b).\sum_{a\leq b}\mu(a,b)X^{\operatorname{ht}(a)}=X^{\operatorname{ht}(b)}{(1-1/X)}^{\operatorname{nz}(b)}.

The result then follows from the definition of KtK_{t}. ∎

In our running example, the MM-triangle is

(1−18113−334506−380112−658−208352−2848815−92201−18864−2078−984015−3419−661)\left(\begin{array}[]{rrrrrrr}1&-18&113&-334&506&-380&112\\ -6&58&-208&352&-284&88&\\ 15&-92&201&-188&64&&\\ -20&78&-98&40&&&\\ 15&-34&19&&&&\\ -6&6&&&&&\\ 1&&&&&&\end{array}\right)

where the south-west to north-east diagonal records the number of elements in PtP_{t} according to height.

2.6 ff-vector and hh-vector

As all intervals in the poset PtP_{t} are products of total orders, the Hasse diagram of PtP_{t} can be viewed as the skeleton of a cubical complex. Let us compute its ff-vector, the polynomial in one variable XX where the coefficient of XkX^{k} is the number of kk-dimensional cubical faces.

Every cubical face is determined by an interval [a,b][a,b] in PtP_{t}. We will gather them according to their top element bb. When bb has nz⁡(b)\operatorname{nz}(b) non-zero coordinates, it contributes by the faces of a nz⁡(b)\operatorname{nz}(b)-dimensional hypercube that are incident to a fixed vertex of this hypercube. The ff-vector is therefore

ft​(X)=∑b∈Pt(1+X)nz⁡(b).f_{t}(X)=\sum_{b\in P_{t}}{(1+X)}^{\operatorname{nz}(b)}. (22)

By (16), this can be computed from the polynomial KtK_{t} as

ft​(X)=Kt​(1+X,1).f_{t}(X)=K_{t}(1+X,1). (23)

The hh-vector of the arbor tt is defined as the generating polynomial

ht​(X)=∑b∈PtXnz⁡(b).h_{t}(X)=\sum_{b\in P_{t}}{X}^{\operatorname{nz}(b)}.

It satisfies ht​(X)=ft​(X−1)=Kt​(X,1)h_{t}(X)=f_{t}(X-1)=K_{t}(X,1). By (21), this implies that

ht​(X)=Mt​(11−X,1−X).h_{t}(X)=M_{t}\left(\frac{1}{1-X},1-X\right). (24)

In our running example, one finds that the ff-vector of PtP_{t} is

ft​(X)=X6+24​X5+186​X4+654​X3+1152​X2+990​X+330f_{t}(X)=X^{6}+24X^{5}+186X^{4}+654X^{3}+1152X^{2}+990X+330

and its hh-vector is

ht​(X)=X6+18​X5+81​X4+130​X3+81​X2+18​X+1,h_{t}(X)=X^{6}+18X^{5}+81X^{4}+130X^{3}+81X^{2}+18X+1,

which is nicely palindromic.

3 Ehrhart-Zeta duality for linear arbors

This section proposes a conjectural duality exchanging Ehrhart polynomials and Zeta polynomials.

Let tt be an arbor such that each vertex of tt has at most one sub-tree. This is called a linear arbor. Still the vertices can contain several elements.

For a linear arbor tt, let Rev⁡(t)\operatorname{Rev}(t) be the reverse of tt, defined as the linear arbor in which the vertices are in the opposite order. This amounts to choose the root vertex of Rev⁡(t)\operatorname{Rev}(t) to be the unique leaf of tt. Reversal is an involution on linear arbors.

For example, here are two arbors tt and Rev⁡(t)\operatorname{Rev}(t), mutually reverse, with their roots on the left.

Conjecture 3.1.

For every linear arbor tt, the Ehrhart polynomial Et​(u)E_{t}(u) of the polytope QtQ_{t} is equal to the shifted Zeta polynomial ZRev⁡(t)​(u+1)Z_{\operatorname{Rev}(t)}(u+1) of the poset PRev⁡(t)P_{\operatorname{Rev}(t)}.

By looking at the leading coefficients, Conjecture 3.1 would identify the normalized volume of QtQ_{t} to the number of maximal chains of PRev⁡(t)P_{\operatorname{Rev}(t)}. Recall that in dimension nn the normalized volume is n!n! times the volume.

By the special case of the value at u=1u=1, the posets of the arbors tt and Rev⁡(t)\operatorname{Rev}(t) should share the same number of elements. Something finer seems to hold.

Conjecture 3.2.

For every linear arbor tt, the hh-vectors of tt and Rev⁡(t)\operatorname{Rev}(t) are equal.

For example, for the two arbors above, both with 501501 elements, one gets

Et\displaystyle E_{t} =u+1720⋅(20167​u5+57230​u4+62225​u3+32170​u2+7848​u+720),\displaystyle=\frac{u+1}{720}\cdot(20167u^{5}+57230u^{4}+62225u^{3}+32170u^{2}+7848u+720),
Zt\displaystyle Z_{t} =u60⋅(2​u−1)⋅(898​u4−1611​u3+1002​u2−249​u+20),\displaystyle=\frac{u}{60}\cdot(2u-1)\cdot(898u^{4}-1611u^{3}+1002u^{2}-249u+20),
ERev⁡(t)\displaystyle E_{\operatorname{Rev}(t)} =u+160⋅(2​u+1)⋅(898​u4+1981​u3+1557​u2+514​u+60),\displaystyle=\frac{u+1}{60}\cdot(2u+1)\cdot(898u^{4}+1981u^{3}+1557u^{2}+514u+60),
ZRev⁡(t)\displaystyle Z_{\operatorname{Rev}(t)} =u720⋅(20167​u5−43605​u4+34975​u3−12795​u2+2098​u−120).\displaystyle=\frac{u}{720}\cdot(20167u^{5}-43605u^{4}+34975u^{3}-12795u^{2}+2098u-120).

The volume of QtQ_{t} is 20167/72020167/720 and the number of maximal chains of PtP_{t} is 2155221552. Conversely, the volume of QRev⁡(t)Q_{\operatorname{Rev}(t)} is 21552/72021552/720 and the number of maximal chains of PRev⁡(t)P_{\operatorname{Rev}(t)} is 2016720167. Both tt and Rev⁡(t)\operatorname{Rev}(t) have hh-vector

x6+23​x5+122​x4+209​x3+122​x2+23​x+1.x^{6}+23x^{5}+122x^{4}+209x^{3}+122x^{2}+23x+1.

Both conjectures have been checked by computer for all linear arbors of size at most 1111. We will not purse these conjectures further here. One may wonder if the first one can be explained by the existence of unimodular triangulations.

4 Transmutation of MM-triangles

Recall from Appendix A that the MM-triangle of a graded poset is the following polynomial:

m=∑a≤bμ⁡(a,b)​Xht⁡(a)​Yht⁡(b),m=\sum_{a\leq b}\mu(a,b)X^{\operatorname{ht}(a)}Y^{\operatorname{ht}(b)},

where μ\mu is the Möbius function of the poset.

Let us introduce the following operation, called transmutation:

m¯​(X,Y)=m⁡(1−Y1−X​Y,1−X​Y).\overline{m}(X,Y)=m\left(\frac{1-Y}{1-XY},1-XY\right). (25)

Transmutation is an involution, as can be checked directly. We will explain later where it comes from.

Note that for the posets PtP_{t}, the MM-triangle MtM_{t} can be computed from the simpler polynomial KtK_{t} as defined in (16). It follows that the transmuted MM-triangle is

M¯t​(X,Y)=Kt​(Y⁡(X−1)1−Y,1−Y).\overline{M}_{t}(X,Y)=K_{t}\left(\frac{Y(X-1)}{1-Y},1-Y\right). (26)

As explained at length in Section 0.1, one of the main motivations for the article is the following hope: there should exist another graded poset 𝖭𝖢t\mathsf{NC}_{t} whose MM-triangle is M¯t\overline{M}_{t}.

For example, consider the arbor tt equal to

.

Then the poset PtP_{t} has 1414 elements. Its MM-triangle and transmuted MM-triangle are

(−16−1053−85−331)and(−510−6110−166−661),\left(\begin{array}[]{rrrr}-1&6&-10&5\\ 3&-8&5&\\ -3&3&&\\ 1&&&\end{array}\right)\quad\text{and}\quad\left(\begin{array}[]{rrrr}-5&10&-6&1\\ 10&-16&6&\\ -6&6&&\\ 1&&&\end{array}\right),

displayed as matrices of coefficients, with the constant term at the bottom left.

One can check that the transmuted MM-triangle is the MM-triangle of the classical lattice of noncrossing-partitions of a set of size 44, as defined in [Kre72].

Proposition 4.1.

The diagonal of the transmuted MM-triangle is the hh-vector of tt.

Proof.

Formula (26) expresses the transmuted MM-triangle as

∑a∈Pt(1−Y)ht⁡(a)−nz⁡(a)​(Y⁡(X−1))nz⁡(a).\sum_{a\in P_{t}}{(1-Y)}^{\operatorname{ht}(a)-\operatorname{nz}(a)}{(Y(X-1))}^{\operatorname{nz}(a)}.

In every monomial in this expression, the power of YY is larger than or equal to the power of XX. The restriction to monomials with equal powers is

∑a∈P(Y​X)nz⁡(a),\sum_{a\in P}{(YX)}^{\operatorname{nz}(a)},

which is equal to Kt​(X​Y,1)K_{t}(XY,1) encoding the hh-vector of tt. ∎

Let us now say a few words about the origin of the transmutation operation.

Closely linked to the MM-triangle, there is another two-variable polynomial called the HH-triangle. They are related by the transformations (58) and (59) recalled in Appendix A.

These triangles and conversion rules between them first appeared in the study of the combinatorics of finite type cluster algebras [Cha04, Cha06]. In this context, the MM-triangle was considered for the noncrossing-partitions lattice attached to an 𝔸​𝔻​𝔼\mathbb{A}\mathbb{D}\mathbb{E}-quiver. The HH-triangle was a natural refinement of the hh-vector of the cluster fan for the same quiver.

One can define transmutation of MM-triangles as the conjugation of transposition on HH-triangles by the conversion maps between HH-triangles and MM-triangles. Here transposition just means, viewing HH-triangles as triangular matrices in the appropriate way, the transposition of matrices.

Note that the HH-triangle can be interpreted as a refined decomposition of the homology groups of a smooth toric variety. In this context, the transposition has no clear meaning, as it exchanges the homological grading with the other additional grading.

5 Unary-binary arbors and quadrangulations

Let us say that an arbor is unary-binary if

  • •

    every vertex has one element and

  • •

    every vertex has at most 2 sub-trees.

We will talk about vertices of valency 00, 11 or 22.

For example, here is a unary-binary arbor:

,

where the valencies of a,b,c,da,b,c,d are 2,0,1,02,0,1,0.

Given such an arbor tt, let us choose a planar embedding and assume that the arbor is drawn with the root on the left and growing to the right as above.

Using this picture, one can define a quiver GtG_{t} as follows. The vertices of GtG_{t} are the vertices of tt. The edges of GtG_{t} are the edges of tt suitably oriented. Let vv be a vertex vv of valency 22. Let αv\alpha_{v} and βv\beta_{v} the two edges between vv and its 22 sub-trees, from top to bottom. We orient αv\alpha_{v} towards vv and βv\beta_{v} from vv outwards. Other edges are oriented arbitrarily.

We now consider GtG_{t} as a quiver-with-relations for the relations αv​βv=0\alpha_{v}\beta_{v}=0 for all vertices vv of valency 22.

For instance, by choosing to orient the remaining arrow from dd to cc, the previous example gives the quiver-with-relations

.

We refer the reader to [ABCJP10, Sch23] for the definition and properties of gentle quivers and algebras. Essentially this means that at every vertex, there are at most two incoming arrows α,α′\alpha,\alpha^{\prime} and at most two outgoing arrows β,β′\beta,\beta^{\prime} and there are relations α​β\alpha\beta and α′​β′\alpha^{\prime}\beta^{\prime} when they make sense.

Lemma 5.1.

The quiver-with-relations GtG_{t} is a gentle quiver.

Proof.

Every vertex is incident to at most 33 edges and there can be no sink and no source vertex. If there are three incident edges, two of them are linked by a relation. ∎

Let us recall briefly now an important construction starting from the gentle quiver GtG_{t}. This comes from τ\tau-tilting theory as introduced in [AIR14]. To every finite-dimensional algebra over a field, one can associate a set of support-τ\tau-tilting objects. These objects then naturally appear as vertices in a regular graph called the mutation graph. It happens, for specific classes of finite-dimensional algebras, that the mutation graph of support-τ\tau-tilting objects is finite. That finiteness and its consequences hold notably for the gentle algebras GtG_{t} that we consider here.

In this case, the mutation graph is in fact oriented and the Hasse diagram of a partial order which is congruence-uniform. There is also a simple polytope whose skeleton is the mutation graph. We refer to [PPP21] for these properties in the case of gentle algebras.

This finite mutation graph on support-τ\tau-tilting objects for the quiver-with-relations GtG_{t} seems to be related to the poset PtP_{t} itself by the following conjecture.

Conjecture 5.2.

The number of support τ\tau-tilting objects for the gentle quiver-with-relations GtG_{t} is equal to the number of elements of the poset PtP_{t}.

In fact, there should be a more precise relationship. Let us consider the spherical simplicial complex S​CtSC_{t} which is the polar dual of the simple polytope attached to GtG_{t} by τ\tau-tilting theory.

Conjecture 5.3.

In the simplicial complex S​CtSC_{t}, there exists a facet CC such that the FF-triangle for the pair (S​Ct,C)(SC_{t},C) coincides with the FF-triangle associated with the transmuted MM-triangle of PtP_{t} by the formulas of Appendix A.

This can been checked concretely in small cases. It has been checked by computer for n≤8n\leq 8.

In our example tt as above, the poset PtP_{t} has 3333 elements. One can check that the gentle quiver GtG_{t} also has 3333 support τ\tau-tilting objects. The FF-triangle associated with the transmuted MM-triangle is

(1446148417231018222510)\left(\begin{array}[]{rrrrr}1&&&&\\ 4&4&&&\\ 6&14&8&&\\ 4&17&23&10&\\ 1&8&22&25&10\end{array}\right) (27)

and it appears as expected for some facet of S​CtSC_{t}.

5.1 Stokes polytopes and quadrangulations

Let us present briefly an alternative description of the same situation, replacing the general τ\tau-tilting theory by the more specific notion of Stokes polytopes and Baryshnikov compatibility [Bar01, Cha16].

Let’s consider a regular polygon with 2​n+42n+4 vertices. Fix a quadrangulation QQ of this polygon, which means a set of nn noncrossing segments joining vertices and cutting the polygon into quadrilateral regions. After Baryhsnikov, one can define a compatibility relation between quadrangulations. On the set RQR_{Q} of quadrangulations compatible with QQ, there is a mutation process, that defines a mutation graph. Moreover, this mutation process is oriented and defines a partial order. The mutation graph is also the skeleton of a polytope, called the Stokes polytope for the quadrangulation [MP19, Man18, BMP17].

There is a simple way to map the planar-embedded arbor tt into a quadrangulation. There is also a way to define a gentle quiver from any quadrangulation. The composite map recovers the definition of GtG_{t} from tt. By this correspondence, the τ\tau-tilting theory exactly matches the combinatorial description using mutations of compatible quadrangulations.

It follows that the conjectural statements above could be rephrased entirely using the structures (mutation graph, poset, polytope) coming from this context instead of those coming from τ\tau-tilting theory.

6 Arbors of type 𝔸\mathbb{A}

In this section, we consider the case of linear arbors with no multiple vertex, so that their shape is a simple chain. This is the intersection of the set of unary-binary arbors considered before with the set of linear arbors. In order to compute the Zeta polynomial and the MM-triangle for the poset PtP_{t} in this case, it is convenient to study a more general familly of posets.

In this section, we will use the following convention: for a product βℓ=∏r=2ℓαr\beta_{\ell}=\prod_{r=2}^{\ell}\alpha_{r}, the value at ℓ=1\ell=1 is 11 and the value at ℓ=0\ell=0 is 1/α11/\alpha_{1}.

Let m≥1m\geq 1 be an integer, used as a slope parameter. Let RmR_{m} be the region in the plane of coordinates (x,y)(x,y) defined by the conditions

0≤x,0≤y,m​y<x.\displaystyle 0\leq x,\quad 0\leq y,\quad my<x. (28)

Let now (x,y)(x,y) be nonnegative integers such that

m​y<x.\displaystyle my<x. (29)

We consider the set of lattice paths in RmR_{m} that go from (0,0)(0,0) to the fixed point (x,y)(x,y), by steps (+1,0)(+1,0) (denoted by 𝖷\mathsf{X}) or (0,+1)(0,+1) (denoted by 𝖸\mathsf{Y}). The point (0,0)(0,0) is the unique allowed point on the line m​y=xmy=x at the boundary of RmR_{m}.

To each lattice path ww in RmR_{m} from (0,0)(0,0) to (x,y)(x,y), one associates a word A=(a1,…,ax−1)A=(a_{1},\ldots,a_{x-1}), that records the lengths of sequences of consecutive 𝖸\mathsf{Y} between two letters 𝖷\mathsf{X}. The letter aia_{i} is the number of 𝖸\mathsf{Y} between the ii-th instance of 𝖷\mathsf{X} and the next one. The length of AA is x−1x-1.

One can characterise the set of such words AA by the following inequalities:

m⁡(∑i≤jai)<j,m\left(\sum_{i\leq j}a_{i}\right)<j, (30)

for 1≤j≤x−11\leq j\leq x-1 and the condition

∑iai≤y.\sum_{i}a_{i}\leq y. (31)

In particular, every aia_{i} for i≤mi\leq m must vanish.

One then defines a poset 𝒫m,x,yF\mathscr{P}^{F}_{m,x,y} by term-wise comparison on this set of words. In this notation, the exponent FF stands for Fuss.

The poset 𝒫m,x,yF\mathscr{P}^{F}_{m,x,y} is graded by the sum of the aia_{i}, that we will denote by ht\operatorname{ht}. There is a unique minimum ⊥\bot, with all aia_{i} being zero. Every interval [⊥,(ai)i][\bot,{(a_{i})}_{i}] is isomorphic to the product of total orders of size ai+1a_{i}+1.

The special case where m=1m=1, x=n+2x=n+2 and y=ny=n recovers the poset PtP_{t} attached to the linear arbor of size nn with no multiple vertex. Indeed, in terms of words (a1,…,an+1)(a_{1},\ldots,a_{n+1}), being strictly below the diagonal x=yx=y amounts to the conditions a1≤0a_{1}\leq 0, a1+a2≤1a_{1}+a_{2}\leq 1, …\ldots, a1+⋯+an+1≤na_{1}+\cdots+a_{n+1}\leq n. Necessarily a1=0a_{1}=0, so that one finds the defining equations of the poset PtP_{t} and the same term-wise comparison.

Lemma 6.1.

Let y≥1y\geq 1. The posets 𝒫m,m​y+1,yF\mathscr{P}^{F}_{m,my+1,y} and 𝒫m,m​y+1,y−1F\mathscr{P}^{F}_{m,my+1,y-1} are isomorphic.

Proof.

For all m≥1m\geq 1 and for all y≥1y\geq 1 and x=m​y+1x=my+1, lattice paths in the region RmR_{m} that ends at (x,y)(x,y) are in bijection, by removal of the last step 𝖸\mathsf{Y}, with lattice paths in the region RmR_{m} that ends at (x,y−1)(x,y-1). This bijection is the identity on the coordinates used to define the partial order. ∎

6.1 Zeta polynomial

Theorem 6.2.

The Zeta polynomial of 𝒫m,x,yF\mathscr{P}^{F}_{m,x,y} is given by

Zm,x,yF​(u)=((x−m​y−1)​(u−1)+1)y!​∏j=2y((x−1)​(u−1)+j).Z^{F}_{m,x,y}(u)=\frac{\bigl((x-my-1)(u-1)+1\bigr)}{y!}\prod_{j=2}^{y}\bigl((x-1)(u-1)+j\bigr). (32)
Proof.

One first notes that if x=1x=1, then y=0y=0 and the right-hand side is the constant polynomial 11. As the poset 𝒫m,1,0F\mathscr{P}^{F}_{m,1,0} is just a singleton, the statement holds in that case.

The rest of the proof is by induction based on this initial case and the next four lemmas. ∎

Let us denote 𝖹𝖾𝗍𝖺m,x,yF​(u)\mathsf{Zeta}^{F}_{m,x,y}(u) the Zeta polynomial of the poset 𝒫m,x,yF\mathscr{P}^{F}_{m,x,y}.

Lemma 6.3.

For all m≥1m\geq 1 and for all y≥1y\geq 1 and x=m​y+1x=my+1, there is a polynomial equality

𝖹𝖾𝗍𝖺m,x,yF​(u)=𝖹𝖾𝗍𝖺m,x,y−1F​(u).\mathsf{Zeta}^{F}_{m,x,y}(u)=\mathsf{Zeta}^{F}_{m,x,y-1}(u). (33)
Proof.

By Lemma 6.1, the posets 𝒫m,x,yF\mathscr{P}^{F}_{m,x,y} and 𝒫m,x,y−1F\mathscr{P}^{F}_{m,x,y-1} are isomorphic. ∎

Lemma 6.4.

For all m≥1m\geq 1 and for all x,yx,y satisfying (29) with x>m​y+1x>my+1, there is a polynomial equality

𝖹𝖾𝗍𝖺m,x,yF​(u)=∑j=0y𝖹𝖾𝗍𝖺m,x−1,y−jF​(u)​(j−2+uj).\mathsf{Zeta}^{F}_{m,x,y}(u)=\sum_{j=0}^{y}\mathsf{Zeta}^{F}_{m,x-1,y-j}(u)\binom{j-2+u}{j}. (34)
Proof.

By polynomiality of Zeta polynomials with respect to uu, it suffices to check the formula when uu is replaced by any integer q≥2q\geq 2. We will use a bijection between chains.

Let us assume q≥2q\geq 2 and consider a chain A1≤A2≤⋯≤Aq−1A_{1}\leq A_{2}\leq\cdots\leq A_{q-1} in 𝒫m,x,yF\mathscr{P}^{F}_{m,x,y}. We denote by aℓ,ia_{\ell,i} for 1≤i≤x−11\leq i\leq x-1 the coordinates of the lattice path AℓA_{\ell}. Note that the chain condition implies that ∑i≤kaℓ,i\sum_{i\leq k}a_{\ell,i} is growing with ℓ\ell for every fixed kk.

Let j=aq−1,x−1j=a_{q-1,x-1}. The possible values of jj are all integers between 00 and yy.

For 1≤ℓ≤q−11\leq\ell\leq q-1, we define A^ℓ\widehat{A}_{\ell} by forgetting the coordinate aℓ,x−1a_{\ell,x-1} in AℓA_{\ell}. Then every A^ℓ\widehat{A}_{\ell} defines an element in 𝒫m,x−1,y−jF\mathscr{P}^{F}_{m,x-1,y-j}. Indeed, the conditions (30) remain trivially true and the condition (31) is implied by the definition of jj and the growth of ∑i<x−1aℓ,i\sum_{i<x-1}a_{\ell,i} as a function of ℓ\ell:

∑i<x−1aℓ,i+j≤∑i<x−1aq−1,i+aq−1,x−1≤y.\sum_{i<x-1}a_{\ell,i}+j\leq\sum_{i<x-1}a_{q-1,i}+a_{q-1,x-1}\leq y.

We therefore get a chain A^1≤A^1≤A^2⋯≤A^q−1\widehat{A}_{1}\leq\widehat{A}_{1}\leq\widehat{A}_{2}\cdots\leq\widehat{A}_{q-1} in 𝒫m,x−1,y−jF\mathscr{P}^{F}_{m,x-1,y-j}.

To build back the original chain A1≤A2≤⋯≤Aq−1A_{1}\leq A_{2}\leq\cdots\leq A_{q-1} from this truncated chain, one has to choose appropriate values aℓ,x−1a_{\ell,x-1} for 1≤ℓ≤q−11\leq\ell\leq q-1.

To recover Aq−1A_{q-1} in 𝒫m,x,yF\mathscr{P}^{F}_{m,x,y}, one can only choose aq−1,x−1=ja_{q-1,x-1}=j. For this choice, the conditions (30) and (31) hold for Aq−1A_{q-1}.

Now choose the other integers aℓ,x−1a_{\ell,x-1} such that 0≤a1,x−1≤⋯≤aq−1,x−1=j0\leq a_{1,x-1}\leq\cdots\leq a_{q-1,x-1}=j. Then the conditions (30) and (31) for AℓA_{\ell} result from those for Aq−1A_{q-1}. So we have indeed built back a chain in 𝒫m,x,yF\mathscr{P}^{F}_{m,x,y}.

For each fixed jj, the number of possible choices for the whole increasing sequence of integers aℓ,x−1a_{\ell,x-1} (1≤ℓ<q−11\leq\ell<q-1) is therefore a binomial coefficient (j+q−2j)\binom{j+q-2}{j}. ∎

Lemma 6.5.

For all m≥1m\geq 1 and for all y≥1y\geq 1 and x=m​y+1x=my+1, there is a polynomial equality

Zm,x,yF​(u)=Zm,x,y−1F​(u).Z^{F}_{m,x,y}(u)=Z^{F}_{m,x,y-1}(u). (35)
Proof.

This is an easy computation using (32). ∎

The following lemma is a computation using hypergeometric functions.

Lemma 6.6.

For all m≥1m\geq 1 and for all x,yx,y satisfying (29) with x≥m​y+1x\geq my+1, there is a polynomial equality

Zm,x,yF​(u)=∑j=0yZm,x−1,y−jF​(u)​(j+u−2j).Z^{F}_{m,x,y}(u)=\sum_{j=0}^{y}Z^{F}_{m,x-1,y-j}(u)\binom{j+u-2}{j}. (36)
Proof.

In the right hand side of (36), let us use the formula (32). One finds

∑j=0y(j+u−2j)​((x−m⁡(y−j)−2)​(u−1)+1)(y−j)!​∏ℓ=2y−j((x−2)​(u−1)+ℓ).\sum_{j=0}^{y}\binom{j+u-2}{j}\frac{\bigl((x-m(y-j)-2)(u-1)+1\bigr)}{(y-j)!}\prod_{\ell=2}^{y-j}\bigl((x-2)(u-1)+\ell\bigr).

Using the shorthands u¯=u−1\overline{u}=u-1 and x¯=x−2\overline{x}=x-2, this becomes

∑j=0y(j+u¯−1j)​((x¯−m⁡(y−j))​u¯+1)(y−j)!​∏ℓ=2y−j(x¯​u¯+ℓ).\sum_{j=0}^{y}\binom{j+\overline{u}-1}{j}\frac{\bigl((\overline{x}-m(y-j))\overline{u}+1\bigr)}{(y-j)!}\prod_{\ell=2}^{y-j}\bigl(\overline{x}\overline{u}+\ell\bigr).

One can separate into two sums:

∑j=0y(j+u¯−1j)​1(y−j)!​∏ℓ=1y−j(x¯​u¯+ℓ)−m​u¯​∑j=0y(j+u¯−1j)​1(y−j−1)!​∏ℓ=2y−j(x¯​u¯+ℓ).\sum_{j=0}^{y}\binom{j+\overline{u}-1}{j}\frac{1}{(y-j)!}\prod_{\ell=1}^{y-j}\bigl(\overline{x}\overline{u}+\ell\bigr)-m\overline{u}\sum_{j=0}^{y}\binom{j+\overline{u}-1}{j}\frac{1}{(y-j-1)!}\prod_{\ell=2}^{y-j}\bigl(\overline{x}\overline{u}+\ell\bigr).

In each of these sums, one can replace the summation upper bound yy by +∞+\infty and get an hypergeometric expression:

1y!​∏ℓ=1y(x¯​u¯+ℓ)⋅F12​(.u¯,−y−y−x¯​u¯.,1)−m​u¯(y−1)!​∏ℓ=2y(x¯​u¯+ℓ)⋅F12​(.u¯,−y+1−y−x¯​u¯.,1).\frac{1}{y!}\prod_{\ell=1}^{y}\bigl(\overline{x}\overline{u}+\ell\bigr)\cdot{}_{2}F_{1}\biggl(\genfrac{.}{.}{0.0pt}{}{\bu,-y}{-y-\bx\bu};1\biggr)-\frac{m\overline{u}}{(y-1)!}\prod_{\ell=2}^{y}\bigl(\overline{x}\overline{u}+\ell\bigr)\cdot{}_{2}F_{1}\biggl(\genfrac{.}{.}{0.0pt}{}{\bu,-y+1}{-y-\bx\bu};1\biggr).

Then using the Chu-Vandermonde formula for each term, one gets

1y!​∏ℓ=1y(x¯​u¯+ℓ)​(−y−x¯​u¯−u¯)y(−y−x¯​u¯)y−m​u¯(y−1)!​∏ℓ=2y(x¯​u¯+ℓ)​(−y−x¯​u¯−u¯)y−1(−y−x¯​u¯)y−1,\frac{1}{y!}\prod_{\ell=1}^{y}\bigl(\overline{x}\overline{u}+\ell\bigr)\frac{{(-y-\overline{x}\overline{u}-\overline{u})}_{y}}{{(-y-\overline{x}\overline{u})}_{y}}-\frac{m\overline{u}}{(y-1)!}\prod_{\ell=2}^{y}\bigl(\overline{x}\overline{u}+\ell\bigr)\frac{{(-y-\overline{x}\overline{u}-\overline{u})}_{y-1}}{{(-y-\overline{x}\overline{u})}_{y-1}},

where one has used some Pochhammer symbols. This can be simplified as

1y!​∏ℓ=1y(x¯​u¯+u¯+ℓ)−m​u¯(y−1)!​∏ℓ=2y(x¯​u¯+u¯+ℓ).\frac{1}{y!}\prod_{\ell=1}^{y}\bigl(\overline{x}\overline{u}+\overline{u}+\ell\bigr)-\frac{m\overline{u}}{(y-1)!}\prod_{\ell=2}^{y}\bigl(\overline{x}\overline{u}+\overline{u}+\ell\bigr).

which is the expected formula (32). ∎

Let tnt_{n} be the linear arbor with nn vertices and no multiple vertex. It follows from the general Theorem 6.2 at m=1,x=n+2,y=nm=1,x=n+2,y=n that the Zeta polynomial of the poset PtnP_{t_{n}} for the arbor tnt_{n} is the same as the known Zeta polynomial of the noncrossing-partitions lattice, first computed by Edelman [Ede80], namely

1n!​∏j=0n−1((n+1)​u−j).\frac{1}{n!}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\bigl((n+1)u-j\bigr).

6.2 MM-triangle

Here we will describe the MM-triangles of the posets 𝒫m,x,yF\mathscr{P}^{F}_{m,x,y}.

Because all intervals between the unique minimum and any element are products of total orders, and by the same reasoning as in Section 2.5, the MM-triangle is the sum

∑p∈𝒫F​(m,x,y)(X​Y)ht⁡(a)​(1−1/X)nz⁡(a),\sum_{p\in\mathscr{P}^{F}(m,x,y)}{(XY)}^{\operatorname{ht}(a)}{(1-1/X)}^{\operatorname{nz}(a)}, (37)

where ht⁡(a)\operatorname{ht}(a) is the sum of coordinates and nz⁡(a)\operatorname{nz}(a) is the number of non-zero coordinates.

Lemma 6.7.

Assume that y>0y>0 and x>1+m​yx>1+my. Then

Mm,x,y=Mm,x−1,y+(1−1/X)​∑j=1y(X​Y)j​Mm,x−1,y−j.M_{m,x,y}=M_{m,x-1,y}+(1-1/X)\sum_{j=1}^{y}{(XY)}^{j}M_{m,x-1,y-j}. (38)
Proof.

Let us define a bijection φ\varphi from 𝒫m,x,yF\mathscr{P}^{F}_{m,x,y} to the disjoint union

⨆j=0y𝒫m,x−1,y−jF.\bigsqcup_{j=0}^{y}\mathscr{P}^{F}_{m,x-1,y-j}.

The map φ\varphi is defined by deleting the subword consisting of the ax−1a_{x-1} steps 𝖸\mathsf{Y} just before the last 𝖷\mathsf{X} step, and also removing that 𝖷\mathsf{X} step. Let jj denote ax−1a_{x-1}. If j=0j=0, then one obtains a path in 𝒫m,x−1,yF\mathscr{P}^{F}_{m,x-1,y} because x>1+m​yx>1+my. Otherwise, jj can take any value between 11 and yy, and then the path obtained after deletion belongs to 𝒫m,x−1,y−jF\mathscr{P}^{F}_{m,x-1,y-j}. All this clearly defines a bijection φ\varphi, as one can insert back the removed subword, depending on jj, just after the last 𝖷\mathsf{X}.

If j=0j=0, the bijection φ\varphi preserves both the height ht\operatorname{ht} and nz\operatorname{nz}. Otherwise, the height ht\operatorname{ht} is decreased by jj and the number nz\operatorname{nz} is decreased by 11. This gives the expected formula, using (37). ∎

Together with the initial conditions

Mm,x,0=1M_{m,x,0}=1 (39)

because there is only one path in 𝒫m,x,0F\mathscr{P}^{F}_{m,x,0} and

Mm,m​y+1,y=Mm,m​y+1,y−1M_{m,my+1,y}=M_{m,my+1,y-1} (40)

because of the isomorphism of Lemma 6.1, this determines everything by induction.

Proposition 6.8.

The MM-triangle of 𝒫m,x,yF\mathscr{P}^{F}_{m,x,y} is the sum of

1ℓ!​(ℓk)​(x−1−m​ℓ)​∏r=2ℓ(x−r+k)​(−X)k​(−Y)ℓ,\frac{1}{\ell!}\binom{\ell}{k}\left(x-1-m\ell\right)\prod_{r=2}^{\ell}(x-r+k){(-X)}^{k}{(-Y)}^{\ell}, (41)

for 0≤k≤ℓ≤y0\leq k\leq\ell\leq y.

Proof.

By induction. The statement holds in the two initial cases by inspection.

Let us expand the right-hand side of (38) as the sum of two sums, with the leftmost term of (38) being incorporated into the first sum:

∑j=0y∑0≤k≤ℓ≤y−j1ℓ!​(ℓk)​(x−2−m​ℓ)​∏r=2ℓ(x−r−1+k)​(−X)k+j​(−Y)ℓ+j\sum_{j=0}^{y}\sum_{0\leq k\leq\ell\leq y-j}\frac{1}{\ell!}\binom{\ell}{k}(x-2-m\ell)\prod_{r=2}^{\ell}(x-r-1+k){(-X)}^{k+j}{(-Y)}^{\ell+j}

and

∑j=1y∑0≤k≤ℓ≤y−j1ℓ!​(ℓk)​(x−2−m​ℓ)​∏r=2ℓ(x−r−1+k)​(−X)k+j−1​(−Y)ℓ+j.\sum_{j=1}^{y}\sum_{0\leq k\leq\ell\leq y-j}\frac{1}{\ell!}\binom{\ell}{k}(x-2-m\ell)\prod_{r=2}^{\ell}(x-r-1+k){(-X)}^{k+j-1}{(-Y)}^{\ell+j}.

After a careful manipulation of sums, one obtains

∑0≤k≤ℓ≤y∑j=0k1(ℓ−j)!​(ℓ−jk−j)​(x−2−m⁡(ℓ−j))​∏r=2ℓ−j(x−r−1+k−j)​(−X)k​(−Y)ℓ\sum_{0\leq k\leq\ell\leq y}\sum_{j=0}^{k}\frac{1}{(\ell-j)!}\binom{\ell-j}{k-j}(x-2-m(\ell-j))\prod_{r=2}^{\ell-j}(x-r-1+k-j){(-X)}^{k}{(-Y)}^{\ell}

and

∑0≤k<ℓ≤y∑j=1k+11(ℓ−j)!​(ℓ−jk−j+1)​(x−2−m⁡(ℓ−j))​∏r=2ℓ−j(x−r+k−j)​(−X)k​(−Y)ℓ.\sum_{0\leq k<\ell\leq y}\sum_{j=1}^{k+1}\frac{1}{(\ell-j)!}\binom{\ell-j}{k-j+1}(x-2-m(\ell-j))\prod_{r=2}^{\ell-j}(x-r+k-j){(-X)}^{k}{(-Y)}^{\ell}.

We will now concentrate on the individual coefficients of (−X)k​(−Y)ℓ{(-X)}^{k}{(-Y)}^{\ell} in these two sums. Each coefficient is an affine function with respect to mm. Let us first handle the constant part w.r.t. mm. Using twice Lemma B.1, one gets the two contributions

1k!​(ℓ−k)!​∏r=1ℓ(x−1−r+k)and1k!​(ℓ−k−1)!​∏r=1ℓ−1(x−1−r+k).\frac{1}{k!(\ell-k)!}\prod_{r=1}^{\ell}(x-1-r+k)\quad\text{and}\quad\frac{1}{k!(\ell-k-1)!}\prod_{r=1}^{\ell-1}(x-1-r+k).

Summing both terms, one gets as expected

1k!​(ℓ−k)!​(x−1)​∏r=2ℓ(x−r+k).\frac{1}{k!(\ell-k)!}(x-1)\prod_{r=2}^{\ell}(x-r+k).

Let us turn to the linear part w.r.t. mm. Removing the factor −m-m and using twice Lemma B.2, one obtains two contributions

1k!​(ℓ−k)!​(x−1)​ℓ−k(x−1)​(x−2)​∏r=1ℓ(x−1−r+k)\frac{1}{k!(\ell-k)!}\frac{(x-1)\ell-k}{(x-1)(x-2)}\prod_{r=1}^{\ell}(x-1-r+k)

and

1k!​(ℓ−k−1)!​(x−1)​(ℓ−1)−k(x−1)​(x−2)​∏r=1ℓ−1(x−1−r+k).\frac{1}{k!(\ell-k-1)!}\frac{(x-1)(\ell-1)-k}{(x-1)(x-2)}\prod_{r=1}^{\ell-1}(x-1-r+k).

Summing both terms gives as expected

ℓk!​(ℓ−k)!​∏r=2ℓ(x−r+k).\frac{\ell}{k!(\ell-k)!}\prod_{r=2}^{\ell}(x-r+k).

∎

The special case m=1m=1 and y=ny=n and x=n+2x=n+2, is related to the linear arbor tnt_{n} of size nn with no multiple vertex.

Proposition 6.9.

The MM-triangle of the poset PtnP_{t_{n}} for the arbor tnt_{n} is

Mn𝔸=∑0≤k≤ℓ≤nn+1−ℓn+k−ℓ+1​(n+kn)​(nℓ−k)​(−X)k​(−Y)ℓ.M^{\mathbb{A}}_{n}=\sum_{0\leq k\leq\ell\leq n}\frac{n+1-\ell}{n+k-\ell+1}\binom{n+k}{n}\binom{n}{\ell-k}{(-X)}^{k}{(-Y)}^{\ell}.

This formula is essentially the same as the FF-triangle for the cluster complex of type 𝔸n\mathbb{A}_{n}. Recall that this FF-triangle is given by [Cha04, Prop. 11]:

Fn𝔸=∑k=0n∑ℓ=0nℓ+1k+ℓ+1​(nk+ℓ)​(n+kn)​Xk​Yℓ.F^{\mathbb{A}}_{n}=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\sum_{\ell=0}^{n}\frac{\ell+1}{k+\ell+1}\binom{n}{k+\ell}\binom{n+k}{n}X^{k}Y^{\ell}. (42)

It follows easily that

Mn𝔸(X,Y)=Fn𝔸(−X,−1/Y)⋅(−Y)n.M^{\mathbb{A}}_{n}(X,Y)=F^{\mathbb{A}}_{n}(-X,-1/Y)\cdot{(-Y)}^{n}. (43)
Proposition 6.10.

The transmuted MM-triangle of 𝒫1,n+2,nF\mathscr{P}^{F}_{1,n+2,n} is the MM-triangle of the poset of noncrossing-partitions of type 𝔸n\mathbb{A}_{n}.

Proof.

The transmutation of Mn𝔸M^{\mathbb{A}}_{n} is

Mn𝔸​(1−Y1−X​Y,1−X​Y)=Fn𝔸​(1−YX​Y−1,1X​Y−1)⋅(X​Y−1)n.M^{\mathbb{A}}_{n}\left(\frac{1-Y}{1-XY},1-XY\right)=F^{\mathbb{A}}_{n}\left(\frac{1-Y}{XY-1},\frac{1}{XY-1}\right)\cdot{(XY-1)}^{n}.

By the proof of the F=MF=M conjecture in [Ath07] and the transformations in Appendix A, the MM-triangle for the poset of noncrossing-partitions of type 𝔸n\mathbb{A}_{n} is given by

N⁡(X,Y)=Fn𝔸​(Y⁡(X−1)1−X​Y,X​Y1−X​Y)⋅(1−X​Y)n.N(X,Y)=F^{\mathbb{A}}_{n}\left(\frac{Y(X-1)}{1-XY},\frac{XY}{1-XY}\right)\cdot{(1-XY)}^{n}.

Because the poset of noncrossing-partitions is self-dual, one has the symmetry
