N⁡(X,Y)=N⁡(1/Y,1/X)⋅(X​Y)n.N(X,Y)=N(1/Y,1/X)\cdot{(XY)}^{n}.

Combining these formulas gives the expected equality. ∎

An explicit formula for the MM-triangle of the poset of noncrossing-partitions of type 𝔸n\mathbb{A}_{n}, not needed here, can be found in [Kra06, Prop. A] with parameter m=1m=1.

Recall that tnt_{n} denotes the arbor of size nn with no multiple vertex. It follows from the previous results that the poset PtnP_{t_{n}} is a transmuted partner of the poset of noncrossing partitions of type 𝔸n\mathbb{A}_{n}. In particular, the hh-vector of tnt_{n} is equal to the hh-vector of the generalized associahedra of type 𝔸n\mathbb{A}_{n}.

7 Arbors of type 𝔹\mathbb{B}

Let n≥1n\geq 1 and k≥0k\geq 0. Let 𝒫n,k𝔹\mathscr{P}^{\mathbb{B}}_{n,k} be the set of nn-tuples (x1,…,xn)(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}) of nonnegative integers with sum less than or equal to kk. This is a poset for term-wise comparison.

The poset 𝒫n,n𝔹\mathscr{P}^{\mathbb{B}}_{n,n} is exactly the poset PtP_{t} attached by the general construction to the arbor with one vertex containing nn elements.

The posets 𝒫n,k𝔹\mathscr{P}^{\mathbb{B}}_{n,k} are graded by the height function ht\operatorname{ht} which is the sum of coordinates. They have a unique minimum element ⊥\bot. The definition of the poset 𝒫n,k𝔹\mathscr{P}^{\mathbb{B}}_{n,k} implies that its intervals are products of total orders.

Lemma 7.1.

In a poset 𝒫n,k𝔹\mathscr{P}^{\mathbb{B}}_{n,k}, the upper ideal generated by any element of height jj is isomorphic to 𝒫n,k−j𝔹\mathscr{P}^{\mathbb{B}}_{n,k-j}.

Proof.

This follows directly from the definition. The bijection is given by substraction of the chosen minimal element. ∎

Theorem 7.2.

The Zeta polynomial of 𝒫n,k𝔹\mathscr{P}^{\mathbb{B}}_{n,k} is equal to (n⁡(u−1)+kk)\binom{n(u-1)+k}{k}.

Proof.

Let us consider a chain e1≤⋯≤eu−1e_{1}\leq\cdots\leq e_{u-1} in 𝒫n,k𝔹\mathscr{P}^{\mathbb{B}}_{n,k}. One can describe the chain by its first element e1e_{1} together with all differences ui+1−uiu_{i+1}-u_{i} for 1≤i≤u−21\leq i\leq u-2. This gives a bijection with (u−1)(u-1)-tuples of nn nonnegative integers whose total sum is less than or equal to kk. The number of these tuples is the expected binomial coefficient. ∎

It follows from the general Theorem 7.2 at k=nk=n that the Zeta polynomial of the poset PtP_{t} for the arbor with just one vertex of cardinality nn is the same as the known Zeta polynomial of the noncrossing-partitions lattice of type 𝔹\mathbb{B}, first computed by Montenegro according to Reiner, see [Mon93, Rei97].

Let us now turn to the MM-triangles of the posets 𝒫n,k𝔹\mathscr{P}^{\mathbb{B}}_{n,k}, namely

Mn,k=∑a≤bμ⁡(a,b)​X|a|​Y|b|.M_{n,k}=\sum_{a\leq b}\mu(a,b)X^{|a|}Y^{|b|}.

As said above, by definition of 𝒫n,k𝔹\mathscr{P}^{\mathbb{B}}_{n,k}, all its intervals are products of total orders. By the same reasoning as in Section 2.5, this leads to the expression

Mn,k=∑a∈𝒫n,k𝔹(X​Y)ht⁡(a)​(1−1/X)nz⁡(a),M_{n,k}=\sum_{a\in\mathscr{P}^{\mathbb{B}}_{n,k}}{(XY)}^{\operatorname{ht}(a)}{(1-1/X)}^{\operatorname{nz}(a)}, (44)

where nz\operatorname{nz} is the number of non-zero coordinates.

In this sum, let us write aa as a pair (j,b)(j,b) where jj is the first coordinate and bb are the remaining coordinates seen as an element in 𝒫n−1,k−j𝔹\mathscr{P}^{\mathbb{B}}_{n-1,k-j}.

By separating the contribution for j=0j=0, this allows to rewrite the sum as

Mn,k=Mn−1,k+(1−1/X)​∑j=1k(X​Y)j​Mn−1,k−j.M_{n,k}=M_{n-1,k}+(1-1/X)\sum_{j=1}^{k}{(XY)}^{j}M_{n-1,k-j}. (45)

Together with the initial condition

M0,k=1M_{0,k}=1 (46)

for the singleton poset, this equation determines the MM-triangle by induction on nn.

Proposition 7.3.

The MM-triangle for the poset 𝒫n,k𝔹\mathscr{P}^{\mathbb{B}}_{n,k} is

∑r=0k∑ℓ=0k−r(ℓ+n−1n−1)​(nr)​(−X)ℓ​(−Y)ℓ+r.\sum_{r=0}^{k}\sum_{\ell=0}^{k-r}\binom{\ell+n-1}{n-1}\binom{n}{r}{(-X)}^{\ell}{(-Y)}^{\ell+r}. (47)
Proof.

This is done by checking that this formula satisfies the induction (45) and the initial condition (46). The initial condition is clear. For the induction step, the right hand side of (45) is the sum of

∑j=0k∑r=0k−j∑ℓ=0k−j−r(ℓ+n−2n−2)​(n−1r)​(−X)ℓ+j​(−Y)ℓ+r+j\sum_{j=0}^{k}\sum_{r=0}^{k-j}\sum_{\ell=0}^{k-j-r}\binom{\ell+n-2}{n-2}\binom{n-1}{r}{(-X)}^{\ell+j}{(-Y)}^{\ell+r+j}

and

∑j=1k∑r=0k−j∑ℓ=0k−j−r(ℓ+n−2n−2)​(n−1r)​(−X)ℓ+j−1​(−Y)ℓ+r+j.\sum_{j=1}^{k}\sum_{r=0}^{k-j}\sum_{\ell=0}^{k-j-r}\binom{\ell+n-2}{n-2}\binom{n-1}{r}{(-X)}^{\ell+j-1}{(-Y)}^{\ell+r+j}.

After replacing the summation variable jj by a new summation variable ℓ′=ℓ+j\ell^{\prime}=\ell+j and some further careful manipulations of summations, they become

∑r=0k∑ℓ′=0k−r(ℓ′+n−1n−1)​(n−1r)​(−X)ℓ′​(−Y)ℓ′+r\sum_{r=0}^{k}\sum_{\ell^{\prime}=0}^{k-r}\binom{\ell^{\prime}+n-1}{n-1}\binom{n-1}{r}{(-X)}^{\ell^{\prime}}{(-Y)}^{\ell^{\prime}+r}

and

∑r=1k∑ℓ′=0k−r(ℓ′+n−1n−1)​(n−1r−1)​(−X)ℓ′​(−Y)ℓ′+r.\sum_{r=1}^{k}\sum_{\ell^{\prime}=0}^{k-r}\binom{\ell^{\prime}+n-1}{n-1}\binom{n-1}{r-1}{(-X)}^{\ell^{\prime}}{(-Y)}^{\ell^{\prime}+r}.

Adding these two expressions then gives the expected expression. ∎

The special case k=nk=n is related to the arbor tnt_{n} with one vertex containing nn elements.

Proposition 7.4.

The MM-triangle of the poset PtnP_{t_{n}} for the arbor tnt_{n} is

Mn,n​(X,Y)=∑r=0n∑ℓ=0n−r(ℓ+n−1n−1)​(nr)​(−X)ℓ​(−Y)ℓ+r.M_{n,n}(X,Y)=\sum_{r=0}^{n}\sum_{\ell=0}^{n-r}\binom{\ell+n-1}{n-1}\binom{n}{r}{(-X)}^{\ell}{(-Y)}^{\ell+r}.

This formula is essentially the same as the FF-triangle for the cluster complex of type 𝔹n\mathbb{B}_{n}. Recall that this FF-triangle is given by [Cha04, Prop. 13]:

Fn𝔹=∑k=0n∑ℓ=0n(nk+ℓ)​(n+k−1n−1)​Xk​Yℓ.F^{\mathbb{B}}_{n}=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\sum_{\ell=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k+\ell}\binom{n+k-1}{n-1}X^{k}Y^{\ell}. (48)

It follows easily that

Mn,n(X,Y)=Fn𝔹(−X,−1/Y)⋅(−Y)n.M_{n,n}(X,Y)=F^{\mathbb{B}}_{n}(-X,-1/Y)\cdot{(-Y)}^{n}. (49)
Proposition 7.5.

The transmuted MM-triangle of 𝒫n,n𝔹\mathscr{P}^{\mathbb{B}}_{n,n} is the MM-triangle of the poset of noncrossing-partitions of type 𝔹n\mathbb{B}_{n}.

Proof.

The transmutation of Mn,nM_{n,n} is

Mn,n​(1−Y1−X​Y,1−X​Y)=Fn𝔹​(1−YX​Y−1,1X​Y−1)⋅(X​Y−1)n.M_{n,n}\left(\frac{1-Y}{1-XY},1-XY\right)=F^{\mathbb{B}}_{n}\left(\frac{1-Y}{XY-1},\frac{1}{XY-1}\right)\cdot{(XY-1)}^{n}.

By the proof of the F=MF=M conjecture in [Ath07] and the conversion formulas in Appendix A, the MM-triangle for the poset of noncrossing-partitions of type 𝔹n\mathbb{B}_{n} is given by

N⁡(X,Y)=Fn𝔹​(Y⁡(X−1)1−X​Y,X​Y1−X​Y)⋅(1−X​Y)n.N(X,Y)=F^{\mathbb{B}}_{n}\left(\frac{Y(X-1)}{1-XY},\frac{XY}{1-XY}\right)\cdot{(1-XY)}^{n}.

Because the poset of noncrossing-partitions is self-dual, one has the symmetry

N⁡(X,Y)=N⁡(1/Y,1/X)⋅(X​Y)n.N(X,Y)=N(1/Y,1/X)\cdot{(XY)}^{n}.

Combining these formulas gives the expected equality. ∎

An explicit formula for the MM-triangle of the poset of noncrossing-partitions of type 𝔹n\mathbb{B}_{n}, not needed here, can be found in [Kra06, Prop. B] with parameter m=1m=1.

It follows that the poset PtnP_{t_{n}} for the arbor tnt_{n} with one vertex containing nn elements is a transmuted partner of the poset of noncrossing partitions of type 𝔹n\mathbb{B}_{n}. In particular, the hh-vector of tnt_{n} is equal to the hh-vector of the generalized associahedra of type 𝔹n\mathbb{B}_{n}.

Let us also record here the following value, useful in the next section.

Proposition 7.6.

For n≥1n\geq 1, let tnt_{n} be the arbor with just one vertex with nn elements. Then

Ktn​(X,Y)=∑0≤j≤k≤n(nj)​(k−1k−j)​Xj​Yk.K_{t_{n}}(X,Y)=\sum_{0\leq j\leq k\leq n}\binom{n}{j}\binom{k-1}{k-j}X^{j}Y^{k}. (50)
Proof.

This is a direct application of Proposition 2.8 in the case without sub-tree. The double sum there is restricted to the unique term ℓ=j\ell=j and m=km=k. ∎

8 Arbors and halohedra

The halohedra form a sequence of simple convex polytopes. They have a topological interpretation as a compactification of a configuration space, similar to the case of associahedra and cyclohedra [DHV11, DFHV12]. They also have a combinatorial description in terms of “design tubings” of the cycle graphs, that makes them close relatives of graph-associahedra. The halohedra have also appeared in mathematical physics [SC18, Sal19].

There is one halohedron HnH_{n} in dimension nn for each dimension n≥1n\geq 1, starting with a segment and a pentagon. The number of vertices of HnH_{n} is

3​n−1n​(2​n−2n−1).\frac{3n-1}{n}\binom{2n-2}{n-1}.

For n≥2n\geq 2, let hnh_{n} be the arbor with n−1n-1 elements in the root vertex plus one leaf with one element.

Proposition 8.1.

For n≥2n\geq 2, the cardinality of PhnP_{h_{n}} is the number of vertices of HnH_{n}.

Proof.

This is done using Proposition 2.1 at m=1m=1, using as starting point the generating polynomial 1+X1+X for the leaf vertex. One finds that the generating polynomial for PtP_{t} with respect to height is

∑j=0n((n+j−2n−2)+(n+j−3n−2))​Xj.\sum_{j=0}^{n}\left(\binom{n+j-2}{n-2}+\binom{n+j-3}{n-2}\right)X^{j}.

This can be evaluated at X=1X=1 to

(2​n−1n−1)+(2​n−2n−1),\binom{2n-1}{n-1}+\binom{2n-2}{n-1},

which is the expected result. ∎

For n≥1n\geq 1, let hn′h^{\prime}_{n} be the arbor with one element in the root vertex plus one leaf with n−1n-1 elements. This is the reverse arbor of hnh_{n}.

Proposition 8.2.

For n≥1n\geq 1, the cardinality of Phn′P_{h^{\prime}_{n}} is the number of vertices of HnH_{n}.

Proof.

This is done using Proposition 2.1 at m=1m=1. For the leaf vertex with n−1n-1 elements, the generating polynomial is

∑j=0n−1(n−2+jn−2)​Xj.\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\binom{n-2+j}{n-2}X^{j}.

One finds that the generating polynomial for PtP_{t} with respect to height is

∑j=0n−1(n−1+jn−1)​Xj+(2​n−2n−1)​Xn.\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\binom{n-1+j}{n-1}X^{j}+\binom{2n-2}{n-1}X^{n}.

At X=1X=1, this simplifies to

(2​n−1n)+(2​n−2n−1),\binom{2n-1}{n}+\binom{2n-2}{n-1},

which is the expected result. ∎

Let us now compute the hh-vectors for these two families of arbors.

Proposition 8.3.

As a polynomial, for n≥2n\geq 2, the hh-vector of hnh_{n} is

∑j=0n−1(n−1j)​(nj)​Xj+∑j=1n(n−1j−1)2​Xj.\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\binom{n-1}{j}\binom{n}{j}X^{j}+\sum_{j=1}^{n}\binom{n-1}{j-1}^{2}X^{j}. (51)
Proof.

One computes Khn​(X,1)K_{h_{n}}(X,1) using Proposition 2.9, with starting point the polynomial 1+X​Y1+XY for the leaf vertex. One gets exactly the expected formula for the coefficient of XjX^{j}. ∎

One can easily check that this polynomial is palindromic.

Proposition 8.4.

As a polynomial, for n≥1n\geq 1, the hh-vector of hn′h^{\prime}_{n} is

∑j=0n−1(n−1j)2​Xj+∑j=1n(n−1j−1)​(nj)​Xj.\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\binom{n-1}{j}^{2}X^{j}+\sum_{j=1}^{n}\binom{n-1}{j-1}\binom{n}{j}X^{j}. (52)
Proof.

One computes Khn​(X,1)K_{h_{n}}(X,1) using Proposition 2.9, with starting point the polynomial from Proposition 7.6. One gets two terms for the coefficient of XjX^{j}. The first one is

∑k=jn−1(n−1j)​(k−1k−j)\sum_{k=j}^{n-1}\binom{n-1}{j}\binom{k-1}{k-j}

for 0≤j≤n−10\leq j\leq n-1, which sums to (n−1j)2\binom{n-1}{j}^{2}. The second term is

∑k=j−1n−1(n−k)​(n−1j−1)​(k−1k−j+1)\sum_{k=j-1}^{n-1}(n-k)\binom{n-1}{j-1}\binom{k-1}{k-j+1}

for 1≤j≤n1\leq j\leq n, which sums to (n−1j−1)​(nj)\binom{n-1}{j-1}\binom{n}{j}. ∎

It follows that the hh-vectors for hnh_{n} and hn′h^{\prime}_{n} coincide, as predicted by Conjecture 3.2.

The hh-vectors for the halohedra are known by [Alm22, Theorem 6.1.11], which says, once slightly adapted, that the generating series of hh-vectors of halohedra for n≥1n\geq 1 is

h=1+(1+X)​s2​1−2​(1+X)​s+(X−1)2​s2−12=(X+1)​s+(X2+3​X+1)​s2+⋯h=\frac{1+(1+X)s}{2\sqrt{1-2(1+X)s+{(X-1)}^{2}s^{2}}}-\frac{1}{2}=(X+1)s+(X^{2}+3X+1)s^{2}+\cdots

as a formal power series in ss. This series therefore satisfies the algebraic equation

(1−2​(1+X)​s+(X−1)2​s2)​(2​h+1)2=(1+(1+X)​s)2,(1-2(1+X)s+{(X-1)}^{2}s^{2}){(2h+1)}^{2}={(1+(1+X)s)}^{2},

which can also be written as

(1−2​(1+X)​s+(X−1)2​s2)​(h+h2)=X​s2+X​s+s.(1-2(1+X)s+{(X-1)}^{2}s^{2})(h+h^{2})=Xs^{2}+Xs+s. (53)

It is proved in Appendix C that the generating series of the common hh-vectors for the two families of arbors considered above satisfies the algebraic equation (53). As they start with the same initial terms, this implies that they coincide with the hh-vectors of the halohedra.

Let us note that halohedra are related to the Coxeter type 𝔻n\mathbb{D}_{n}: for n≥2n\geq 2, the hh-vector for HnH_{n} is equal, as a polynomial in XX, to the sum of the hh-vector for the associahedra of type 𝔻n\mathbb{D}_{n}, with XX times the hh-vector for the associahedra of type 𝔸n−2\mathbb{A}_{n-2} (see [FR07, Fig. 5.12] for the necessary formulas).

9 Hochschild polytopes

The Hochschild polytopes11 1 They are also known as freehedra in anglo-greek. were introduced by Saneblidze in the context of algebraic topology of loop spaces [San09, RS18]. They form a sequence of simple polytopes, one in each dimension n≥1n\geq 1, starting with a segment in dimension 11 and a pentagon in dimension 22. The Hochschild polytope in dimension nn has 2n−2×(n+3)2^{n-2}\times(n+3) vertices and its hh-vector is (X+1)n−2​(X2+(n+1)​X+1){(X+1)}^{n-2}(X^{2}+(n+1)X+1) [Com21].

In the study of greedy Tamari lattices in [Cha20b], a lattice structure has been introduced on the vertices of each Hochschild polytope, in such a way that cover relations are edges of the polytope. These Hochschild lattices have been studied in detail in [Com21], who showed that they are congruence-uniform. Some further work can be found in [Pol20, Pol21, Müh22, PP24].

Let us consider the following sequence of arbors tnt_{n} for n≥1n\geq 1. The arbor tnt_{n} is made of a root vertex with one element, on which are grafted n−1n-1 vertices, all with one element. Here is the example of t4t_{4}:

.

The Hochschild polytope in dimension nn is related to the poset PtnP_{t_{n}} by the following equalities.

Proposition 9.1.

The number of vertices in the Hochschild polytope in dimension nn is the number of elements of the poset PtnP_{t_{n}}. The hh-vector of the Hochschild polytope is equal to the hh-vector of tnt_{n}.

Proof.

Using the recursive description of the Ehrhart polynomial at m=1m=1 in Proposition 2.1 and the initial value F∘,1=1+XF_{\circ,1}=1+X for the arbor with one vertex, one finds that the number of elements of PtnP_{t_{n}} is

∑ℓ=0n−1(n+1−ℓ)​(n−1ℓ).\sum_{\ell=0}^{n-1}(n+1-\ell)\binom{n-1}{\ell}.

By breaking this sum into two, one gets (n+1)​2n−1−(n−1)​2n−2(n+1)2^{n-1}-(n-1)2^{n-2}. For the finer statement about the hh-vectors, one uses the recursive description in Proposition 2.9 and the initial value K∘=1+X​YK_{\circ}=1+XY for the arbor with one vertex. One first gets that

Ktn​(X,1)=∑j=0n−1(n−1j)​Xj+∑1≤j≤n(n−j+1)​(n−1j−1)​Xj.K_{t_{n}}(X,1)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\binom{n-1}{j}X^{j}+\sum_{1\leq j\leq n}(n-j+1)\binom{n-1}{j-1}X^{j}.

These two simple sums can be computed as above and the result follows. ∎

In fact, there should be a more precise relationship. Let us consider the spherical simplicial complex S​CnSC_{n} which is the polar dual of the Hochschild polytope in dimension nn.

Conjecture 9.2.

In the simplicial complex S​CnSC_{n}, there exists a facet CC such that the FF-triangle for the pair (S​Cn,C)(SC_{n},C) coincides with the FF-triangle associated with the transmuted MM-triangle of PtnP_{t_{n}}.

This can been checked concretely in small cases. It has been checked by computer for n≤9n\leq 9. For n≥3n\geq 3, there seems to be exactly 44 facets with the expected property.

Moreover, it seems that the core-label-order of the Hochschild lattice of dimension nn could be a transmuted partner of the poset PtnP_{t_{n}}. The coincidence of the Zeta polynomial with that of PtnP_{t_{n}} and the transmutation property for MM-triangles have been checked by computer up to n=9n=9.

Using FriCAS [Fri24], one can guess the following conjectural formulas for various generating series in ss for the arbors tnt_{n}. For the Zeta polynomials of the posets PtnP_{t_{n}}:

1+∑n≥1𝖹tn​(u,1)​sn=?exp⁡(∫u(1−u​s)​(1+s−u​s)​𝑑s).1+\sum_{n\geq 1}\mathsf{Z}_{t_{n}}(u,1)s^{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle?}}{{=}}\exp\left(\int\frac{u}{(1-us)(1+s-us)}ds\right).

For the MM-triangles of the posets PtnP_{t_{n}}:

1+∑n≥1Mtn​(X,Y)​sn=?(X​Y​s−Y​s−1)​(X​Y​s−1)(2​X​Y​s−Y​s−1)​(X​Y​s−Y​s+s−1).1+\sum_{n\geq 1}M_{t_{n}}(X,Y)s^{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle?}}{{=}}\frac{{\left(XYs-Ys-1\right)}{\left(XYs-1\right)}}{{\left(2\,XYs-Ys-1\right)}{\left(XYs-Ys+s-1\right)}}.

For the Ehrhart polynomials of the polytopes QtnQ_{t_{n}}:

1+∑n≥1Ehrtn⁡(u)​sn=?12​(1−s(u​s+s−1)−s−1(u​s+s−1)2).1+\sum_{n\geq 1}\operatorname{Ehr}_{t_{n}}(u)s^{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle?}}{{=}}\frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{s}{{\left(us+s-1\right)}}-\frac{s-1}{{\left(us+s-1\right)}^{2}}\right).

For the Laplace transform of volume functions of the polytopes QtnQ_{t_{n}}:

∑n≥1Ltn​(E,V)​sn=?V⁡(sE​V​s−V​s+1+E​sE​s−1).\sum_{n\geq 1}L_{t_{n}}(E,V)s^{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle?}}{{=}}V\left(\frac{s}{EVs-Vs+1}+\frac{Es}{Es-1}\right).

Appendix A Conversion formulas

We gather here the conversion formulas that we use between three different kinds of polynomials in two variables, namely FF-triangles, MM-triangles and HH-triangles. These triangles and rational change-of-variables between them were introduced in [Cha04, Cha06] in the context of cluster fans and generalized associahedra. They are called triangles because of the shape of their Newton polygons. Each triangle comes with a size parameter nn, which is the maximal value of either coordinate in the Newton polygon.

Given a pure simplicial complex of spherical topology S​CSC and a chosen facet CC, one can define the FF-triangle as the following sum over all faces:

F⁡(X,Y)=∑s∈S​CXposi⁡(s)​Ynega⁡(s),F(X,Y)=\sum_{s\in SC}X^{\operatorname{posi}(s)}Y^{\operatorname{nega}(s)}, (54)

where nega⁡(s)\operatorname{nega}(s) (resp. posi⁡(s)\operatorname{posi}(s)) is the number of elements in ss that belong (resp. do not belong) to CC.

Given a graded poset PP, one can define the MM-triangle of PP as the following sum of Möbius numbers weighted using the rank function ht\operatorname{ht}:

M⁡(X,Y)=∑a≤bμ⁡(a,b)​Xht⁡(a)​Yht⁡(b).M(X,Y)=\sum_{a\leq b}\mu(a,b)X^{\operatorname{ht}(a)}Y^{\operatorname{ht}(b)}. (55)

The MM-triangles and FF-triangles are converted to each other by

F⁡(X,Y)=M⁡(YY−X,Y−X1+Y)⋅(1+Y)n,F(X,Y)=M\left(\frac{Y}{Y-X},\frac{Y-X}{1+Y}\right)\cdot{(1+Y)}^{n}, (56)

where nn is the size parameter, and the similar birational formula

M⁡(X,Y)=F⁡(Y⁡(X−1)1−X​Y,X​Y1−X​Y)⋅(1−X​Y)nM(X,Y)=F\left(\frac{Y(X-1)}{1-XY},\frac{XY}{1-XY}\right)\cdot{(1-XY)}^{n} (57)

in the other direction.

We will not define here the HH-triangles, that are related to the cohomology ring of the normal fan of the generalized associahedra. We give the following formulas because they motivate the definition of transmutation, as explained at the end of Section 4.

The MM-triangles and HH-triangles are converted to each other by

m⁡(X,Y)=h⁡((X−1)​Y/(1−Y),X/(X−1))⋅(1−Y)nm(X,Y)=h\bigl((X-1)Y/(1-Y),X/(X-1)\bigr)\cdot{(1-Y)}^{n} (58)

where nn is the size parameter, and the similar birational formula

h⁡(X,Y)=m⁡(Y/(Y−1),(Y−1)​X/(1+(Y−1)​X))⋅(1+(Y−1)​X)nh(X,Y)=m\bigl(Y/(Y-1),(Y-1)X/(1+(Y-1)X)\bigr)\cdot{(1+(Y-1)X)}^{n} (59)

for the conversion in the other way.

Appendix B Two summation lemmas

These lemmas are used in Section 6.

Lemma B.1.

One has

∑j≥01(k−j)!​∏r=2ℓ−j(x−r+k−j)=1k!​1x−1​∏r=1ℓ(x−r+k).\sum_{j\geq 0}\frac{1}{(k-j)!}\prod_{r=2}^{\ell-j}(x-r+k-j)=\frac{1}{k!}\frac{1}{x-1}\prod_{r=1}^{\ell}(x-r+k). (60)
Proof.

Write the left hand side as the value at j=0j=0, namely

1k!​∏r=2ℓ(x−r+k),\frac{1}{k!}\prod_{r=2}^{\ell}(x-r+k),

times the hypergeometric series

F12​(.−k,1−k+2−x.,1).{}_{2}F_{1}\biggl(\genfrac{.}{.}{0.0pt}{}{-k,1}{-k+2-x};1\biggr).

The later evaluates to x+k−1x−1\frac{x+k-1}{x-1} by Chu-Vandermonde. ∎

Lemma B.2.

One has

∑j≥01(k−j)!​(ℓ−j)​∏r=2ℓ−j(x−r+k−j)=1k!​x​ℓ−kx⁡(x−1)​∏r=1ℓ(x−r+k).\sum_{j\geq 0}\frac{1}{(k-j)!}(\ell-j)\prod_{r=2}^{\ell-j}(x-r+k-j)=\frac{1}{k!}\frac{x\ell-k}{x(x-1)}\prod_{r=1}^{\ell}(x-r+k). (61)
Proof.

Write the left hand side as the value at j=0j=0, namely

1k!​ℓ​∏r=2ℓ(x−r+k),\frac{1}{k!}\ell\prod_{r=2}^{\ell}(x-r+k),

times the hypergeometric series

F23​(.−k,1,1−ℓ−k+2−x,−ℓ.,1).{}_{3}F_{2}\biggl(\genfrac{.}{.}{0.0pt}{}{-k,1,1-\ell}{-k+2-x,-\ell};1\biggr).

This hypergeometric series can be transformed22 2 We trust SageMath or Maxima here. This should follow from some contiguity relation. into

F12​(.−k,1−k+2−x.,1)−kℓ⁡(k+x−2)​F12​(.1−k,2−k−x+3.,1).{}_{2}F_{1}\biggl(\genfrac{.}{.}{0.0pt}{}{-k,1}{-k+2-x};1\biggr)-\frac{k}{\ell(k+x-2)}{}_{2}F_{1}\biggl(\genfrac{.}{.}{0.0pt}{}{1-k,2}{-k-x+3};1\biggr).

The later evaluates to (−k+ℓ​x)​(x+k−1)ℓ​x​(x−1)\frac{(-k+\ell x)(x+k-1)}{\ell x(x-1)} by Chu-Vandermonde. ∎

Appendix C Some computations for halohedra

Following Proposition 8.3, let us define two power series in the variable ss:

A=∑n≥1∑j=1n(n−1j−1)2​Xj​snandB=∑n≥1∑j=0n−1(n−1j)​(nj)​Xj​sn.A=\sum_{n\geq 1}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\binom{n-1}{j-1}^{2}X^{j}s^{n}\quad\text{and}\quad B=\sum_{n\geq 1}\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\binom{n-1}{j}\binom{n}{j}X^{j}s^{n}. (62)

The aim of this section is to prove that A+BA+B coincide with the known generating function for hh-vectors of halohedra, characterized by (53) and its first few terms. This is done with the help of the software FriCAS [Fri24] and the ore_algebra package for sagemath [KJJ15, The25].

Let us write PP for the polynomial (X−1)2​s2−2​(X+1)​s+1{(X-1)}^{2}s^{2}-2(X+1)s+1.

First, one can guess an algebraic equation satisfied by AA:

P​A2=X2​s2.PA^{2}=X^{2}s^{2}. (63)

The operator s∂ss\partial_{s} acts on both sides by multiplication by 22. After division by 2​A2A, one deduces a possible differential equation for AA:

s​P​∂sA+(X​s+s−1)​A=0,sP\partial_{s}A+(Xs+s-1)A=0,

with initial condition A0=0A_{0}=0. This is equivalent to the following possible recurrence for the coefficients of AA:

(X−1)2​n​An−(X+1)​(2​n+1)​An+1+(n+1)​An+2=0,{(X-1)}^{2}nA_{n}-(X+1)(2n+1)A_{n+1}+(n+1)A_{n+2}=0,

with initial conditions A0=0A_{0}=0 and A1=XA_{1}=X. One then checks that the formula (62) for AnA_{n} indeed satisfies this recurrence with the same initial conditions. So AA is the unique power series solution of (63) with zero constant term.

Let us now turn to the case of BB. First, one can guess an algebraic equation satisfied by BB:

P⁡(B+B2)=s.P(B+B^{2})=s. (64)

One can also guess a differential equation for BB:

X​s−s+1+2​(X​s−s+1)​B+(X​s−s−1)​P​∂sB=0Xs-s+1+2(Xs-s+1)B+(Xs-s-1)P\partial_{s}B=0

with initial condition B0=0B_{0}=0. Let us consider in the ring ℚ⁡[X,s,B,∂sB]\mathbb{Q}[X,s,B,\partial_{s}B] the ideal generated by (64), its formal derivative with respect to ss and this differential equation. Computing the elimination ideal with respect to ∂sB\partial_{s}B gives back the principal ideal generated by (64). This proves that the differential equation is compatible with (64). This differential equation is equivalent to the following possible recurrence for the coefficients of BB:

(X−1)3​n​Bn−(X−1)​(3​n​X+n+3​X−1)​Bn+1+(3​n​X+n+6​X+4)​Bn+2−(n+3)​Bn+3=0,{(X-1)}^{3}nB_{n}-(X-1)(3nX+n+3X-1)B_{n+1}\\ +(3nX+n+6X+4)B_{n+2}-(n+3)B_{n+3}=0,

with initial conditions B0=0B_{0}=0, B1=1B_{1}=1 and B2=1+2​XB_{2}=1+2X.

One then checks that the formula (62) for BnB_{n} indeed satisfies this recurrence with the same initial conditions. So one can conclude that BB is the unique power series solution of (64) with the given initial terms.

From the algebraic equations (63) and (64), one gets similar equations for A/sA/s and B/sB/s. One then obtains by elimination an algebraic equation for the sum (A+B)/s(A+B)/s, hence

P⋅((A+B)+(A+B)2)=X​s2+(X+1)​s.P\cdot((A+B)+{(A+B)}^{2})=Xs^{2}+(X+1)s. (65)

Note that this requires choosing the correct factor among two in the reducible polynomial for (A+B)/s(A+B)/s obtained by elimination. This is done by identifying the constant term.

This implies the expected equality between A+BA+B and the generating series of hh-vectors of halohedra defined by (53), after checking enough initial terms.
